posts.title: Power BI Embedded Pricing (and Cheaper Alternatives)
posts.description: What Power BI Embedded costs in 2026, checked on Microsoft's own pages: A SKUs, Fabric F SKUs, the F64 licensing threshold, a worked monthly estimate for a small SaaS, and the alternatives worth pricing next to it.
posts.body:
Power BI Embedded is billed by capacity, not by viewer: you rent a block of compute by the hour, and every embedded report your customers open runs on it. On Microsoft's pricing pages for the East US region in US dollars, checked on 9 November 2026, the smallest Azure Power BI Embedded SKU (A1) is $1.0081 an hour, or $735.91 a month if it runs all the time, and the smallest Microsoft Fabric capacity (F2), which can also serve embedded reports, is $0.36 an hour, or $262.80 a month. Add a Power BI Pro license at $14 a user per month (paid yearly) for each person who publishes reports. If you embed for your own customers ("app owns data"), the people viewing the reports need no Power BI license at all.

## Power BI Embedded pricing table

All prices are Microsoft list prices for East US in USD, read on 9 November 2026. Monthly figures are Microsoft's, based on 730 hours. Prices vary by region and currency.

### Azure Power BI Embedded (A SKUs)

Source: [Azure Power BI Embedded pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/power-bi-embedded/)

| SKU | v-cores | Memory | Per hour | Per month (730 h) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | 1 | 3 GB | $1.0081 | $735.91 |
| A2 | 2 | 5 GB | $2.0081 | $1,465.91 |
| A3 | 4 | 10 GB | $4.0242 | $2,937.67 |
| A4 | 8 | 25 GB | $8.0565 | $5,881.25 |
| A5 | 16 | 50 GB | $16.121 | $11,768.33 |
| A6 | 32 | 100 GB | $32.2506 | $23,542.94 |
| A7 | 64 | 200 GB | N/A in East US | N/A in East US |
| A8 | 128 | 400 GB | N/A in East US | N/A in East US |

The page says usage "is computed to the second and billed hourly", and that you aren't charged while the service is paused. There is no commitment.

### Microsoft Fabric capacity (F SKUs)

Source: [Microsoft Fabric pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/microsoft-fabric/)

| SKU | Capacity units | Pay-as-you-go per hour | Pay-as-you-go per month | 1-year reservation per month |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F2 | 2 | $0.36 | $262.80 | $156.33 |
| F4 | 4 | $0.72 | $525.60 | $312.67 |
| F8 | 8 | $1.44 | $1,051.20 | $625.33 |
| F16 | 16 | $2.88 | $2,102.40 | $1,250.67 |
| F32 | 32 | $5.76 | $4,204.80 | $2,501.33 |
| F64 | 64 | $11.52 | $8,409.60 | $5,002.67 |
| F128 | 128 | $23.04 | $16,819.20 | $10,005.33 |
| F256 | 256 | $46.08 | $33,638.40 | $20,010.67 |

Sizes run up to F8192, and Microsoft labels the reservation "~41% savings". Pay-as-you-go works out to $0.18 per capacity unit per hour, the same rate as the "Power BI Capacity Usage" meter in Microsoft's [Azure Retail Prices API](https://prices.azure.com/api/retail/prices?$filter=serviceName%20eq%20'Microsoft%20Fabric'%20and%20armRegionName%20eq%20'eastus').

Microsoft's [capacity and SKUs page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/developer/embedded/embedded-capacity) maps the two families: F8 is equivalent to A1, F16 to A2, F32 to A3 and F64 to A4. F2 and F4 have no A SKU equivalent. Every F SKU supports "embed for your customers".

### Power BI Premium per capacity (P and EM SKUs)

Microsoft no longer sells new P SKUs. The [Premium to Fabric migration overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/support/premium-migration-overview) says each P SKU subscription "ends at the end of its current agreement term". Customers with an active Enterprise Agreement can renew until the agreement ends. EM and A SKUs "aren't part of this retirement". The [Premium overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/enterprise/powerbi/service-premium-what-is) says EM SKUs need a yearly commitment, and that EM1 and EM2 are sold only through volume licensing. None of the Microsoft pages I checked publish an EM price.

### Per-user licenses

Source: [Power BI pricing](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-fabric/features/power-bi/pricing). The same page lists Power BI Embedded as "Variable" with a "Contact sales" link.

| License | Price | Where it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Power BI Pro | $14.00 per user per month, paid yearly | Needed to publish content, and for every viewer when you embed for your organization on anything smaller than F64 |
| Premium Per User (PPU) | $24.00 per user per month, paid yearly | An alternative to Pro for those same viewers, with larger models and 48 refreshes a day |

## How the cost model works in practice

### Capacity, not seats

You pay for a capacity size, and every embedded view, query and refresh uses it. Over the CPU limit, the [Premium overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/enterprise/powerbi/service-premium-what-is) says a Power BI Embedded capacity "throttles its interactive operations": reports slow down rather than the bill going up. For A SKUs, Microsoft documents an autoscale pattern: Azure Monitor alerts trigger a runbook that calls the Capacities Update API to move up or down a SKU.

### Who needs a license

This is the rule that decides most budgets. The [capacity and SKUs page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/developer/embedded/embedded-capacity) says:

- **Embed for your customers (app owns data):** "there are no licensing requirements for the end users." Your app authenticates to Power BI, usually with a service principal, and your customers never see a Power BI login.
- **Embed for your organization (user owns data), Teams, SharePoint:** on A SKUs or any F SKU below F64, "a Pro license or Premium Per User (PPU) is required for each user who will view the embedded content." At F64 and above, free users can view.
- **Publishing:** you need a Pro or PPU account to publish content, unless a service principal publishes through the REST API.

So the F64 threshold matters when you embed for staff. It doesn't matter when you embed for customers.

### Pausing

You can pause A SKUs from the portal, PowerShell or the REST API, and billing stops while they're paused. The catch is in Microsoft's own wording on the [pricing page](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/power-bi-embedded/): "When the service is paused the embedded content will not load." For a customer-facing product, pausing only helps if there are hours when nobody logs in. You can pause F SKUs too, but the [Fabric pause docs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/enterprise/pause-resume) say that at pause time, remaining smoothed operations and overages "are summed, and added to your Azure bill".

### What drives the size you need

Microsoft's [capacity planning guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/developer/embedded/embedded-capacity-planning) gives no "users per SKU" figure, and the current version has no renders-per-hour table. It lists what to consider: your data models, "the number and complexity of required queries", "the hourly distribution of your application usage", and data refresh rates. The method it recommends is a load test. Use the Power BI Capacity Load Assessment Tool "with up to a few dozen concurrent simulated users and extrapolate", then watch CPU in the Fabric Capacity Metrics app. Move up a size if CPU nears the limit.

Memory sets a hard floor. From the [semantic model SKU limits](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/enterprise/powerbi/service-premium-what-is):

| SKU | Max memory per semantic model | Max memory per query | Live connections per second | DirectQuery connections per model |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F2 / F4 | 3 GB | 1 GB | 2 | 5 |
| F8 (A1) | 3 GB | 1 GB | 3.75 | 10 |
| F16 (A2) | 5 GB | 2 GB | 7.5 | 10 |
| F32 (A3) | 10 GB | 5 GB | 15 | 10 |
| F64 (A4) | 25 GB | 10 GB | 30 | 50 |

A refresh can use more than twice the model's size, because the old copy keeps serving queries while the new one loads. Budget for that headroom.

### Dev/test vs production

For development, Microsoft allows "free embed trial tokens with a Pro license", which show a "Free trial version" banner. Production needs a purchased capacity. A small A SKU for staging, paused outside working hours, keeps test costs down.

## Worked example: a small SaaS embedding dashboards for customers

Assume a B2B SaaS with 300 customer users, a handful of dashboards on an imported model under 3 GB, two people building reports, and customers spread across time zones, so the capacity runs 24/7. This is the app-owns-data scenario, so customers need no licenses. All prices are East US list prices from the tables above.

**Option 1: A1, pay as you go**

- Capacity: $1.0081 × 730 hours = $735.91
- Authors: 2 × Pro at $14.00 = $28.00
- **Total: $763.91 a month**

**Option 2: F2, pay as you go (cheapest entry)**

- Capacity: $0.36 × 730 hours = $262.80
- Authors: 2 × $14.00 = $28.00
- **Total: $290.80 a month**

F2 has a quarter of F8's capacity units and 1 GB of memory per query, so load test it before customers use it.

**Option 3: F8 (the A1 equivalent) on a 1-year reservation**

- Capacity: $625.33 a month
- Authors: $28.00
- **Total: $653.33 a month**, with a year's commitment.

**If load tests push you to A2:** $1,465.91 + $28.00 = $1,493.91 a month.

**If your customers are all in one region** and you can pause A1 for 8 hours a night: $1.0081 × 16 hours × 30 days = $483.89, plus $28.00 = $511.89 a month. The cost is that the dashboards don't load for 8 hours.

None of these totals include the database behind the model, gateways, or the engineering time to build the embed flow.

For contrast, take 150 staff viewers under "embed for your organization". F32 plus Pro for every viewer is $4,204.80 + (150 × $14.00) = $6,304.80 a month. F64 with free viewers is $8,409.60 pay-as-you-go, or $5,002.67 on a 1-year reservation. There, licensing decides the size.

## Cheaper or different alternatives

Every price below was read on the vendor's own pricing page on 9 November 2026.

- **[Metabase](https://www.metabase.com/pricing?use_case=ea).** The open-source edition supports guest (view-only) embedding, per the [embedding docs](https://www.metabase.com/docs/latest/embedding/introduction). Pro is $575 a month, cloud or self-hosted, and includes 10 users, then $12 per user per month. Metabase notes that "users of your embeds" count as users. Enterprise starts at $20,000 a year. At 300 customer users on Pro: $575 + (290 × $12) = $4,055 a month. *Pick it when* you want a mature open-source BI tool, and either view-only embeds are enough or your viewer count is small.
- **[Cube](https://cube.dev/pricing).** Cube Core is open source (Apache 2.0 backend, MIT client, per the [GitHub repo](https://github.com/cube-js/cube)). On Cube Cloud, embedded dashboards start at Premium: $80 per developer per month, Viewer seats at $20 per user per month, and a dedicated deployment at $1.20 an hour. *Pick it when* you want a semantic layer and APIs in front of your warehouse and plan to draw the charts yourself.
- **[Luzmo](https://www.luzmo.com/pricing).** One plan, "starting from €1,995 per month", billed annually, with the price scaling with customer adoption. *Pick it when* you want white-label embedded dashboards built for SaaS, with self-service for your customers.
- **[Embeddable](https://embeddable.com/pricing).** A flat monthly subscription with unlimited usage. Pricing on request. *Pick it when* you want code-level control of the components and a predictable bill.
- **Apache Superset / [Preset](https://preset.io/pricing/).** Superset is Apache 2.0 and ships an [embedded SDK](https://github.com/apache/superset/tree/master/superset-embedded-sdk) that uses guest tokens. On Preset, Professional is $20 per user per month billed annually ($25 monthly). Embedding is an add-on that needs Embedded Dashboard Viewer Licenses "starting at $500/month for 50 licenses". *Pick it when* you want open-source BI with embedding, and either self-host it or pay for a managed version.
- **[Sisense](https://www.sisense.com/plans/).** Self-serve and Enterprise plans; no prices published. Pricing on request. *Pick it when* you need regulated-industry compliance, on-prem deployment, or its Compose SDK.
- **[GoodData](https://www.gooddata.ai/pricing/).** Professional is priced per workspace ("platform fee + number of workspaces") with unlimited users. Pricing on request. *Pick it when* you have many tenants with many users each and per-seat pricing would hurt.

### The code-first route

The other option is to skip the BI tool: put an API in front of your warehouse and draw the charts in your own React components. There are no viewer licenses or capacity SKUs. You pay for your database and your app servers, and you write the dashboard UI yourself. That trade is reasonable when analytics is a core product feature and your team already ships frontend code. It's a poor trade when you need non-developers to build reports.

On ClickHouse, [hypequery](/embedded-analytics) is one way to build that layer. It's an open-source TypeScript and Python library that runs in your own backend. You define semantic datasets with measures and dimensions, serve them as typed HTTP endpoints with tenant scope taken from your auth context, read them with React hooks, and expose the same datasets to agents over MCP. It doesn't draw charts or host anything. See [hypequery vs Metabase](/compare/hypequery-vs-metabase) for an honest look at when a BI tool is the better choice, and [ClickHouse multi-tenant analytics](/clickhouse-multi-tenant-analytics) for the tenant isolation patterns.

## When Power BI Embedded is the right choice

Power BI Embedded is often the sensible pick, even at these prices:

- **You're already a Microsoft shop.** Azure billing, Entra ID and an existing Microsoft agreement make procurement easy, and Fabric spend can count toward a Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment.
- **The reports already exist.** If your analysts have built Power BI reports for internal use, embedding them for customers is mostly plumbing, not a rebuild.
- **The people writing reports aren't developers.** Power BI Desktop is free, and analysts can change a report without a code release.
- **You rely on DAX, Power Query or paginated reports.** Those are hard to replace with a custom API.
- **Your viewer count is large and spiky.** Capacity pricing doesn't charge per viewer, so at a few hundred customer users an A1 can cost less than per-user embedding plans.

It's a weaker fit when the embedded report has to look and behave like the rest of your UI, or when your data lives in ClickHouse and you'd rather not maintain a separate Power BI model on top of it.

## FAQ

### How much does Power BI Embedded cost per month?

In East US on 9 November 2026: from $735.91 a month for an always-on A1, or $262.80 for a Fabric F2, plus $14 a month (paid yearly) per Pro license for report authors.

### Do my customers need Power BI licenses to view embedded reports?

Not when you embed for your customers (app owns data). When you embed for your organization, every viewer needs Pro or PPU unless you're on F64 or larger.

### Can I pause Power BI Embedded to save money?

Yes. A SKUs stop billing while paused, but embedded content won't load, so this mainly helps dev, test and staging capacities.

### Should I buy an A SKU or an F SKU?

Pay-as-you-go, the A SKU is cheaper at the same size: A1 is $735.91 a month against $1,051.20 for F8. A 1-year F8 reservation ($625.33) beats both. F SKUs also come smaller (F2, F4) and include the other Fabric workloads.

### Is Power BI Premium per capacity still sold?

No new P SKUs are sold. Existing subscriptions run to the end of their term, and Enterprise Agreement customers can renew until the agreement ends. EM and A SKUs aren't affected.

## Sources

All checked on 9 November 2026. Prices are East US, USD, list.

- [Microsoft Fabric pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/microsoft-fabric/)

- [What is Power BI Premium?](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/fabric/enterprise/powerbi/service-premium-what-is)
- [Power BI Premium to Microsoft Fabric migration overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/support/premium-migration-overview)
- [Pause and start Power BI Embedded capacity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-bi/developer/embedded/azure-pbie-pause-start)

posts.title: chDB in Python: from in-process queries to a metrics API
posts.description: A working chDB tutorial for Python: install it, query Parquet, CSV and pandas with ClickHouse SQL, keep MergeTree tables on disk, then run the same metric definitions on chDB and on a ClickHouse server.
posts.body:
chDB is the ClickHouse database engine packaged as a Python library, so ClickHouse SQL runs inside your Python process with no server to install or connect to. Install it with `pip install chdb` and run a query with `chdb.query("SELECT version()")`. It reads Parquet, CSV and pandas DataFrames, keeps MergeTree tables on disk between runs, and has been part of ClickHouse since March 2024 ([announcement](https://clickhouse.com/blog/chdb-joins-clickhouse-family)).

Everything below was run on chDB 4.4.0 (ClickHouse engine 26.9.2.1), Python 3.14 on macOS, and every output is copied from the terminal. The last part runs one set of metric definitions on chDB and then on a ClickHouse 26.6 server, with the same results.

## How do you install chDB and run a first query?

Install chDB from PyPI with `pip install chdb`, then call `chdb.query()` with a SQL string. The [chDB README](https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb) lists Python 3.9+ on macOS and Linux (x86_64 and ARM64); the PyPI wheels for 4.4.0's engine package, `chdb-core` 26.9.0, cover exactly those four platforms, with no Windows build.

```bash
pip install chdb
```

```python
import chdb

print(chdb.__version__)
print(chdb.query("SELECT version() AS engine, 1 + 1 AS two"))
```

```text
4.4.0
"26.9.2.1",2
```

The first line is the Python package version and the second is the ClickHouse engine version inside it. chDB 4.4.0 installs `chdb-core`, pandas and pyarrow as dependencies. The engine is large: the installed `chdb` package took 366 MB on disk on macOS arm64, which matters if you deploy to a size-limited target such as a serverless function.

## What is chDB used for?

chDB is used where you want ClickHouse SQL without running a ClickHouse server. The cases this guide works through:

- Querying Parquet, CSV and DataFrames from a script or notebook with ClickHouse SQL and functions.
- Test suites and CI jobs that need a real ClickHouse engine. The pytest fixture below creates a MergeTree table in memory, and the test passed in 0.42 seconds with no container.
- Local development on an on-disk database, with queries that later run unchanged on a ClickHouse server.
- Small services and serverless functions, as long as the deployment can carry the engine's size (366 MB installed, measured above) and runs one process per database.

If you already run a ClickHouse server and only need a client, use a driver such as `clickhouse-connect` instead. chDB runs the engine in your process; a driver talks to a server.

## Which output formats can chdb.query return?

`chdb.query(sql, format)` returns CSV text by default, and the second argument takes a ClickHouse output format name, such as `"JSONEachRow"` or `"PrettyCompact"`, or one of two Python-specific ones, `"DataFrame"` (pandas) and `"ArrowTable"` (pyarrow). The README says chDB reads and writes "Parquet, CSV, JSON, Arrow, ORC and 60+" formats.

```python
import chdb

print(chdb.query(
    "SELECT toStartOfMonth(toDate('2026-11-08')) AS month, formatReadableSize(1048576) AS size",
    "PrettyCompact",
))

df = chdb.query("SELECT number, number * 2 AS doubled FROM numbers(3)", "DataFrame")
print(df)

table = chdb.query("SELECT number FROM numbers(3)", "ArrowTable")
print(table.schema)
```

```text
   ┌──────month─┬─size─────┐
1. │ 2026-11-01 │ 1.00 MiB │
   └────────────┴──────────┘

   number  doubled
0       0        0
1       1        2
2       2        4
number: uint64 not null
```

`toStartOfMonth`, `formatReadableSize` and the `numbers()` table function are ClickHouse built-ins, and they work unchanged because the engine is ClickHouse. Use `"PrettyCompact"` while exploring, `"DataFrame"` when the next step is pandas, and `"ArrowTable"` when you want typed columns without a pandas copy: the `uint64` column above keeps the ClickHouse `UInt64` type.

## How do you query Parquet and CSV files with chDB?

Pass the path to the `file()` table function and chDB infers the schema from the file. To have something to query, write a five-row orders table to both formats with pandas:

```python
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "id": ["o1", "o2", "o3", "o4", "o5"],
    "country": ["NZ", "NZ", "AU", "AU", "US"],
    "status": ["paid", "paid", "paid", "refunded", "paid"],
    "amount": [120.50, 80.00, 200.00, 50.00, 310.25],
    "created_at": pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-09-01 10:00:00", "2026-09-02 11:30:00", "2026-09-02 12:00:00",
        "2026-09-03 09:15:00", "2026-09-04 16:45:00",
    ]),
})
orders.to_parquet("/tmp/orders.parquet", index=False)
orders.to_csv("/tmp/orders.csv", index=False)
```

`DESCRIBE` shows what chDB inferred, and the file then works like a table in `FROM`:

```python
import chdb

print(chdb.query(
    "DESCRIBE file('/tmp/orders.parquet') SETTINGS describe_compact_output = 1",
    "PrettyCompact",
))

print(chdb.query("""
    SELECT country, count() AS orders, sum(amount) AS revenue
    FROM file('/tmp/orders.parquet')
    WHERE status = 'paid'
    GROUP BY country
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""", "PrettyCompact"))

print(chdb.query("""
    SELECT toDate(created_at) AS day, sum(amount) AS revenue
    FROM file('/tmp/orders.csv', 'CSVWithNames')
    GROUP BY day
    ORDER BY day
""", "PrettyCompact"))
```

```text
   ┌─name───────┬─type───────────────────────────┐
1. │ id         │ Nullable(String)               │
2. │ country    │ Nullable(String)               │
3. │ status     │ Nullable(String)               │
4. │ amount     │ Nullable(Float64)              │
5. │ created_at │ Nullable(DateTime64(6, 'UTC')) │
   └────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

   ┌─country─┬─orders─┬─revenue─┐
1. │ US      │      1 │  310.25 │
2. │ NZ      │      2 │   200.5 │
3. │ AU      │      1 │     200 │
   └─────────┴────────┴─────────┘

   ┌────────day─┬─revenue─┐
1. │ 2026-09-01 │   120.5 │
2. │ 2026-09-02 │     280 │
3. │ 2026-09-03 │      50 │
4. │ 2026-09-04 │  310.25 │
   └────────────┴─────────┘
```

Inferred columns come back `Nullable`, and the money column is `Float64` because that is what pandas wrote. When exact types matter, load the file into a table with an explicit schema, as in the session section below. The second argument to `file()` names the format; `CSVWithNames` reads the first line as column names. The [file table function docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/table-functions/file) cover globs and the other arguments.

## How do you query a pandas DataFrame with chDB?

Wrap the DataFrame variable in the `Python()` table function: `SELECT ... FROM Python(df)`. chDB looks up the variable `df` by name and queries it as a table.

```python
import chdb
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("/tmp/orders.parquet")

out = chdb.query("""
    SELECT status, count() AS orders, avg(amount) AS avg_amount
    FROM Python(df)
    GROUP BY status
    ORDER BY status
""", "DataFrame")
print(out)
print(out.dtypes)
```

```text
     status  orders  avg_amount
0      paid       4    177.6875
1  refunded       1     50.0000
status            str
orders         uint64
avg_amount    float64
dtype: object
```

Writing the bare name (`FROM df`) failed in chDB 4.4.0 with `Unknown table expression identifier 'df'` when I ran it as a script, so use `Python(df)`. `count()` arrives as `uint64` because ClickHouse returns `UInt64` for counts.

## How do you keep tables between chDB queries?

Open a connection with `chdb.connect(path)`. Tables you create through it live in that directory and are there the next time any process opens it. Plain `chdb.query()` calls don't share tables: a table created in one call was gone in the next, which failed with `Unknown table expression identifier 't'`. Use a connection for anything with `CREATE TABLE`.

```python
import chdb

conn = chdb.connect("/tmp/shop.chdb")
conn.query("""
    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders
    (
        id String,
        country LowCardinality(String),
        status LowCardinality(String),
        amount Decimal(12, 2),
        created_at DateTime64(3, 'UTC')
    )
    ENGINE = MergeTree
    ORDER BY (created_at, id)
""")
conn.query("INSERT INTO orders SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/orders.parquet')")

print(conn.query(
    "SELECT engine, total_rows FROM system.tables WHERE name = 'orders'",
    "PrettyCompact",
))

cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE country = 'NZ' ORDER BY id")
print(cur.fetchall())
conn.close()
```

```text
   ┌─engine────┬─total_rows─┐
1. │ MergeTree │          5 │
   └───────────┴────────────┘

(('o1', Decimal('120.5')), ('o2', Decimal('80')))
```

The `INSERT ... SELECT` converts the Parquet file's nullable floats into the table's `Decimal(12, 2)` column, and the cursor returns them as Python `Decimal`. A second Python process that opens `/tmp/shop.chdb` and runs `SELECT count() FROM orders` gets `5`. Pass `":memory:"` instead of a path for a database that disappears when the last connection closes.

The older `chdb.session.Session(path)` API still works in 4.4.0. In the package source it wraps the same connection class that `chdb.connect` returns, so pick either; this guide uses `connect`.

Three limits showed up while testing:

- One database path per process. With `/tmp/shop.chdb` open, connecting to a second path raised `EmbeddedServer already initialized with path '/tmp/shop.chdb', cannot connect with different path`. It worked after closing the first connection.
- One process per on-disk database. A second process that opened `/tmp/shop.chdb` while the first held it failed with `Error initializing EmbeddedServer`.
- The directory is a ClickHouse data directory. chDB uses the same storage format as `clickhouse local` ([ClickHouse blog](https://clickhouse.com/blog/chdb-joins-clickhouse-family)), and `clickhouse local --path /tmp/shop.chdb` read the table above with the same totals.

## How do you run the same metrics on chDB and on a ClickHouse server?

Define the metrics once in code, then choose the engine when you create the executor. With hypequery's Python SDK, a dataset declares dimensions and measures over a table, and the same dataset runs on chDB (tests, notebooks, CI) or on a ClickHouse server (production) by swapping one constructor. Install it with the `chdb` extra, plus `clickhouse` for the server driver:

```bash
pip install "hypequery[chdb,clickhouse]==0.1.0b3"
```

The dataset, in `metrics.py` (a name that won't clash with the `datasets` package if you have it installed):

```python
from hypequery.datasets import dataset, dimension, formula, measure

orders = dataset(
    "orders",
    source="orders",
    time_key="created_at",
    dimensions={
        "country": dimension.string(),
        "status": dimension.string(),
        "createdAt": dimension.timestamp(column="created_at"),
    },
    measures={
        "revenue": measure.sum("amount"),
        "orderCount": measure.count("id"),
        "averageOrderValue": measure.derived(
            formula.divide("revenue", formula.null_if_zero("orderCount")),
        ),
    },
)
```

A script that runs a query against whichever engine the environment points at:

```python
import os

from hypequery.datasets import DatasetQuery, create_dataset_client, filter, order
from hypequery.execution import (
    ClickHouseConnection,
    create_chdb_executor,
    create_clickhouse_executor,
)

from metrics import orders


def make_executor():
    if os.environ.get("CLICKHOUSE_URL"):
        return create_clickhouse_executor(ClickHouseConnection.from_env())
    return create_chdb_executor("/tmp/shop.chdb")


query = DatasetQuery(
    dimensions=("country",),
    measures=("revenue", "orderCount", "averageOrderValue"),
    filters=(filter.eq("status", "paid"),),
    order_by=(order.desc("revenue"),),
)

with make_executor() as executor:
    analytics = create_dataset_client(executor=executor)
    for row in analytics.execute(orders, query).data:
        print(row)
```

On chDB, reading the `/tmp/shop.chdb` table from the previous section:

```text
{'country': 'US', 'revenue': '310.25', 'orderCount': 1, 'averageOrderValue': 310.25}
{'country': 'NZ', 'revenue': '200.50', 'orderCount': 2, 'averageOrderValue': 100.25}
{'country': 'AU', 'revenue': '200.00', 'orderCount': 1, 'averageOrderValue': 200.0}
```

For the production half I started a local ClickHouse 26.6.2 server, created the same `orders` table with the same five rows through `clickhouse client`, and ran the unchanged script with one environment variable set:

```bash
CLICKHOUSE_URL=clickhouse://default@127.0.0.1:18123/default python run.py
```

```text
{'country': 'US', 'revenue': '310.25', 'orderCount': 1, 'averageOrderValue': 310.25}
{'country': 'NZ', 'revenue': '200.50', 'orderCount': 2, 'averageOrderValue': 100.25}
{'country': 'AU', 'revenue': '200.00', 'orderCount': 1, 'averageOrderValue': 200.0}
```

The rows match, including types: the `Decimal` sum comes back as a string with its scale, the count as `int` and the derived ratio as `float`, as the [execution docs](/docs/python/datasets/execution) describe. A daily breakdown, `DatasetQuery(by="day", measures=("revenue", "orderCount"))`, converted with `result.to_pandas()`, also gave identical frames on both engines, with `period` as `datetime64[us, UTC]`, `revenue` as `float64` and `orderCount` as `Int64`.

To see what runs, `analytics.to_sql(orders, query)` prints the compiled statement. For revenue and average order value by country:

```text
SELECT `__hq_base`.`country` AS `country`, sum(`__hq_base`.`amount`) AS `revenue`, (toFloat64(sum(`__hq_base`.`amount`)) / NULLIF(count(`__hq_base`.`id`), 0)) AS `averageOrderValue` FROM `orders` AS `__hq_base` WHERE `__hq_base`.`status` = <p0:String> GROUP BY `country`
```

`<p0:String>` is a ClickHouse query parameter: the value travels separately from the SQL on both engines.

### Using chDB as a pytest fixture

An in-memory chDB database makes a test fixture with no container. Keep the executor open for the test's lifetime, because closing the last connection discards an in-memory database:

```python
import chdb
import pytest

from hypequery.datasets import DatasetQuery, create_dataset_client
from hypequery.execution import create_chdb_executor

from metrics import orders


@pytest.fixture
def analytics():
    with create_chdb_executor() as executor:  # in-memory
        setup = chdb.connect(":memory:")
        setup.query("""
            CREATE TABLE orders (
                id String, country String, status String,
                amount Decimal(12, 2), created_at DateTime64(3, 'UTC')
            ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id
        """)
        setup.query("""
            INSERT INTO orders VALUES
                ('o1', 'NZ', 'paid', 120.50, '2026-09-01 10:00:00'),
                ('o2', 'NZ', 'refunded', 80.00, '2026-09-02 11:30:00')
        """)
        setup.close()
        yield create_dataset_client(executor=executor)


def test_revenue_by_status(analytics):
    result = analytics.execute(
        orders, DatasetQuery(dimensions=("status",), measures=("revenue",))
    )
    assert sorted(result.data, key=lambda r: r["status"]) == [
        {"status": "paid", "revenue": "120.50"},
        {"status": "refunded", "revenue": "80.00"},
    ]
```

```text
1 passed in 0.42s
```

### Load files into tables before pointing a dataset at them

hypequery runs every dataset query with the ClickHouse setting `readonly = 1`, and ClickHouse refuses the `file()` table function in that mode, even behind a view:

```python
import chdb

conn = chdb.connect(":memory:")
conn.query("CREATE VIEW orders_file AS SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/orders.parquet')")
print(conn.query("SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders_file", "CSV"))
try:
    conn.query("SELECT sum(amount) FROM orders_file SETTINGS readonly = 1")
except Exception as e:
    print(e)
```

```text
760.75

Code: 164. DB::Exception: default: Cannot execute query in readonly mode. (READONLY)
```

A dataset over that view fails the same way. Copy the file into a MergeTree table with `INSERT ... SELECT FROM file(...)`, as in the session section, and point the dataset's `source` at the table. That also matches production, where the data lives in tables. The [chDB page in the Python docs](/docs/python/datasets/chdb) covers in-memory and on-disk paths and how the chDB executor differs from the server one.

## chDB vs DuckDB: which embedded engine should you use?

Choose chDB when your production data is in ClickHouse or will be, and DuckDB when it isn't and you want its dialect, ecosystem or Windows support. Both run analytical SQL inside the Python process ([DuckDB describes itself](https://duckdb.org/) as "in-process").

| | chDB 4.4.0 | DuckDB |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL dialect | ClickHouse SQL and its function library | "based on PostgreSQL" ([DuckDB docs](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/sql/dialect/overview)) |
| Table engines | ClickHouse engines, including MergeTree (shown above) | DuckDB's own storage |
| Path to a ClickHouse server | Same SQL; the data directory opens with `clickhouse local` | A separate engine with its own dialect |
| Python wheels | macOS and Linux, x86_64 and ARM64 | Includes Windows (`win_amd64`, `win_arm64` wheels for 2.0.0 on PyPI) |
| Other languages | Go, Rust, Node.js, Bun, C and C++ ([ClickHouse docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/chdb)) | See [duckdb.org](https://duckdb.org/) |

The main reason to pick chDB is what this guide showed: a query you write and test against chDB is ClickHouse SQL, so it runs on a ClickHouse server without translation, and the `numbers()` and `toStartOfMonth` calls above need no changes. If you test against DuckDB and deploy to ClickHouse, you maintain two dialects. If you never touch ClickHouse, that advantage disappears, and DuckDB's Windows wheels and [extensions](https://duckdb.org/docs/stable/extensions/overview) may matter more. I didn't run benchmarks for this guide, so there are no speed claims here; measure on your own data.

## How do you turn chDB metrics into an API?

Mount hypequery's Serve API in a FastAPI app over an async chDB executor, and the dataset above becomes an HTTP endpoint. This ran locally with FastAPI 0.162.2 and uvicorn 0.54.0:

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI
from hypequery.datasets import create_async_dataset_client
from hypequery.execution import create_async_chdb_executor
from hypequery.serve import (
    HttpSecurity, Principal, ServeRequest, create_api, from_context, to_asgi_app,
)

from metrics import orders

executor = create_async_chdb_executor("/tmp/shop.chdb")
client = create_async_dataset_client(executor=executor)


def developer(request: ServeRequest) -> Principal:
    # Local development only: replace with jwt_strategy or your own auth.
    return Principal(subject="developer")


api = create_api(
    auth=from_context(developer, same_origin=False),
    client=client,
    datasets={"orders": orders},
    security=HttpSecurity(allowed_hosts=("127.0.0.1", "localhost")),
    client_mount_path="/analytics",
)


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    yield
    await executor.aclose()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
app.mount("/analytics", to_asgi_app(api))
```

Save it as `main.py` next to `metrics.py`. FastAPI and uvicorn aren't part of the earlier install, so add them, start the server, and query it from another terminal:

```bash
pip install fastapi "hypequery[server]==0.1.0b3"
uvicorn main:app --port 8000
```

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/analytics/datasets/orders/query \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"dimensions": ["country"], "measures": ["revenue", "orderCount"],
       "filters": [{"field": "status", "operator": "eq", "value": "paid"}],
       "orderBy": [{"field": "revenue", "direction": "desc"}]}'
```

```text
{"data":[{"country":"US","revenue":"310.25","orderCount":"1"},{"country":"NZ","revenue":"200.50","orderCount":"2"},{"country":"AU","revenue":"200.00","orderCount":"1"}]}
```

Over HTTP every measure is a string, `orderCount` included, as the [measures docs](/docs/python/datasets/measures) state. For production, swap in `create_async_from_sync_clickhouse_executor(ClickHouseConnection.from_env())` and real authentication, and run one server process: chDB's on-disk lock means several workers can't share the database. The [FastAPI guide](/clickhouse-fastapi) and the [FastAPI docs page](/docs/python/fastapi) cover JWT auth and calling the client from your own routes.

## Related

- [ClickHouse with Python](/clickhouse-python)
- [A semantic layer in Python](/python-semantic-layer)
- [hypequery Python docs](/docs/python)
- [Embedded ClickHouse (chDB) in the Python docs](/docs/python/datasets/chdb)
- [Introducing hypequery for Python](/blog/introducing-hypequery-python)
- [chDB on GitHub](https://github.com/chdb-io/chdb) and the [chDB docs on clickhouse.com](https://clickhouse.com/docs/chdb)

posts.title: How to Create a Materialized View in ClickHouse: TO Table, POPULATE and Backfill
posts.description: Create an incremental materialized view in ClickHouse the production way: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW ... TO a target table, backfill existing rows safely with a cutoff, avoid POPULATE's gaps, and change, list or drop views. Every query checked on ClickHouse 26.6.
posts.body:
To create a materialized view in ClickHouse, create the target table first, then run `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW view_name TO target_table AS SELECT ... FROM source_table`. From then on, every insert into the source table runs the `SELECT` on the inserted rows and writes the result to the target. Rows that were in the source before the view existed are not processed, so you backfill them yourself with `INSERT INTO target_table SELECT ...` bounded by a cutoff time, because `POPULATE` can miss rows inserted while it runs on ClickHouse 26.6.

For the mental model and the wider list of pitfalls, read the main [guide to materialized views in ClickHouse](/blog/a-guide-to-materialized-views-in-clickhouse); for scheduled views, see [refreshable materialized views](/blog/clickhouse-refreshable-materialized-views). Every statement below was run on ClickHouse 26.6.

## How do you create a materialized view in ClickHouse?

Create a target table with the columns and engine you want, then create the view with `TO` pointing at it. Match the `SELECT` aliases to the target's column names: on 26.6 a `SELECT` column with no matching target column fails the `CREATE` with `THERE_IS_NO_COLUMN`, and target columns the `SELECT` leaves out get their default values.

```sql
CREATE TABLE page_events
(
    ts DateTime,
    user_id UInt32,
    page String,
    duration_ms UInt32
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY (page, ts);

INSERT INTO page_events VALUES
    ('2026-11-06 09:15:00', 1, '/', 120),
    ('2026-11-06 10:02:00', 2, '/', 340),
    ('2026-11-07 14:30:00', 1, '/pricing', 90),
    ('2026-11-08 08:45:00', 3, '/', 200);

CREATE TABLE page_views_daily
(
    day Date,
    page String,
    views UInt64
)
ENGINE = SummingMergeTree
ORDER BY (day, page);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW page_views_daily_mv
TO page_views_daily
AS SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views
FROM page_events
GROUP BY day, page;

SELECT count() FROM page_views_daily;
```

```text
0
```

The four existing events are not in the target. Now insert one more:

```sql
INSERT INTO page_events VALUES ('2026-11-08 17:00:00', 4, '/pricing', 60);

SELECT day, page, views FROM page_views_daily ORDER BY day, page;
```

```text
2026-11-08  /pricing  1
```

Only the row inserted after `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW` reached the target. The [CREATE VIEW reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/view) describes materialized views as working more like insert triggers: they transform each inserted block, and changes to existing source data (updates, deletes, dropped partitions) do not change the view.

## Why use TO instead of the implicit .inner table?

Without `TO`, you must give the view an `ENGINE`, and ClickHouse stores the result in a hidden table that it owns. In an Atomic database the hidden table is named `.inner_id.<uuid>`:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_inner_mv
ENGINE = SummingMergeTree
ORDER BY day
AS SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, count() AS views
FROM page_events
GROUP BY day;

SELECT name, engine FROM system.tables WHERE database = currentDatabase() ORDER BY name;
```

```text
.inner_id.9ba0e383-ea97-49bb-b488-353c293993fa  SummingMergeTree
daily_inner_mv                                  MaterializedView
page_events                                     MergeTree
page_views_daily                                SummingMergeTree
page_views_daily_mv                             MaterializedView
```

`DROP VIEW daily_inner_mv` removed both the view and the `.inner_id` table, and with it all the aggregated data. With `TO`, the view and the data are separate objects, which matters in practice:

| | `TO target_table` | Implicit `.inner_id` table |
|---|---|---|
| `DROP VIEW` | Drops the view; the target and its rows stay | Drops the view and its data |
| Recreate the view with a new query | Target data is kept | Data is lost unless you copy it first |
| Several views writing to one table | Yes; two views pointing `TO dst` both wrote rows | No, each view has its own inner table |
| Target schema and engine | A normal table you created and can `ALTER` | Defined in the view's `ENGINE` clause |
| `ALTER ... MODIFY QUERY` | Supported | The docs call its use "very limited" |

One thing to watch with `TO`: the target must exist for as long as the view does. After `DROP TABLE dst` with the view still attached, `INSERT INTO src VALUES (3)` failed with `Code: 60 ... Target table 'a.dst' of view ... doesn't exists. (UNKNOWN_TABLE)`, and the source row was not written either. Drop the view before its target.

## What does POPULATE do, and can it miss rows?

`POPULATE` runs the view's `SELECT` over the whole source table once at creation time and writes the result into the view. On ClickHouse 26.6 it has two limits that make it a poor fit for production tables.

First, it does not work with `TO`:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW m TO dst POPULATE AS SELECT x FROM src;
```

```text
Code: 62. DB::Exception: When creating a materialized view you can't declare
both 'TO [db].[table]' and 'POPULATE'. (SYNTAX_ERROR)
```

Second, population is not atomic in 26.6. The ClickHouse [26.8 release post](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-release-26-08) says a race condition caused `POPULATE` to skip records inserted during the population, and that 26.8 fixed it with a new setting, `materialized_views_populate_atomically`, on by default. The same release allowed `POPULATE` together with `TO`. The [backfilling guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/clickhouse/data-modelling/backfilling) still recommends `POPULATE` only for small datasets with ingest paused, since it runs over all the data in one query and can fail on interruptions or memory limits.

To find out which behaviour your server has, look for the setting:

```sql
SELECT name, value
FROM system.settings
WHERE name = 'materialized_views_populate_atomically';
```

On 26.6 this returns no rows, which means `POPULATE` can miss rows inserted while it runs. Even where the setting exists, the current CREATE VIEW reference says the guarantee only covers inserts that arrive at the same server, and that `POPULATE` is not supported in ClickHouse Cloud. The manual backfill below works on every version.

## How do you backfill a materialized view with existing data?

Pick a cutoff time a few minutes in the future, create the view with `WHERE ts >= cutoff`, wait until the cutoff has passed, then insert everything before the cutoff into the target yourself. The view handles rows at or after the cutoff and the backfill handles rows before it, so each row is counted once. This is the pattern in ClickHouse's [backfilling guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/clickhouse/data-modelling/backfilling).

Starting from the same four historical events, with a new empty `page_views_daily` and a cutoff of `2026-11-09 00:00:00`, first check that no existing rows are at or after the cutoff. The view will never see those rows and the backfill excludes them, so this query must return 0:

```sql
SELECT count() FROM page_events WHERE ts >= '2026-11-09 00:00:00';
```

Then create the view, let time pass the cutoff, and backfill:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW page_views_daily_mv
TO page_views_daily
AS SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views
FROM page_events
WHERE ts >= '2026-11-09 00:00:00'
GROUP BY day, page;

-- rows that arrive after the view exists but before the cutoff
INSERT INTO page_events VALUES
    ('2026-11-08 18:10:00', 5, '/', 80),
    ('2026-11-08 23:59:00', 8, '/pricing', 75);

-- rows after the cutoff: the view handles these
INSERT INTO page_events VALUES
    ('2026-11-09 00:05:00', 6, '/', 150),
    ('2026-11-09 07:30:00', 7, '/pricing', 400);

-- once the cutoff has passed: backfill everything before it
INSERT INTO page_views_daily
SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views
FROM page_events
WHERE ts < '2026-11-09 00:00:00'
GROUP BY day, page;

SELECT
    (SELECT count() FROM page_events) AS raw_total,
    (SELECT sum(views) FROM page_views_daily) AS target_total;
```

```text
raw_total  target_total
8          8
```

All eight events are counted: four from before the view, two that arrived between creating the view and the cutoff, and two after it. The backfill query is the view's `SELECT` with the filter reversed.

The order matters. In a second run I did the backfill right after creating the view, before the cutoff had passed, and then inserted the same rows. The result was `raw_total 8, target_total 6`: the two events from 18:10 and 23:59 were older than the cutoff, so the view skipped them, and they did not exist yet when the backfill ran.

Running the backfill twice is the other way to get it wrong. A second identical `INSERT INTO page_views_daily SELECT ...` took `target_total` from 8 to 14 (six pre-cutoff events counted again), because `SummingMergeTree` adds the duplicate counts together. If a backfill slice fails partway, don't truncate the target: it also holds the rows the live view wrote. Delete only the failed slice's days and rerun that slice, for example `ALTER TABLE page_views_daily DELETE WHERE day = '2026-11-06'`. That is safe for days that end before the cutoff, because the view's filter means it never writes them; the day the cutoff falls on holds rows from both, so recompute it last, from the source, after the cutoff has passed. Alternatively, backfill into a separate staging table with the same schema and insert from it into the target once every slice has succeeded.

For large tables, run the backfill in slices (one day, or one partition, per statement) so that each statement reads less data and a failure only costs one slice:

```sql
INSERT INTO page_views_daily
SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views
FROM page_events
WHERE ts >= '2026-11-06 00:00:00' AND ts < '2026-11-07 00:00:00'
GROUP BY day, page;
```

The backfilling guide also describes inserting the history into a table with the `Null` engine that has a copy of the view attached, so the view transforms it block by block the same way it handles live inserts, without storing the raw rows a second time.

This procedure assumes no rows older than the cutoff arrive while the backfill runs. A late row for 6 November that arrives after the 6 November slice has finished is skipped by the view, because of its filter, and missed by the slice, and changing the view afterwards does not bring it back. If your data can arrive late, either hold late ingestion until the backfill is done, or reconcile afterwards: for each day before the cutoff that may have received late rows, delete that day from the target and insert it again from the source. Once the backfill and any reconciliation are finished, remove the cutoff filter with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY` (covered below) so later late rows are counted.

## How do you aggregate with SummingMergeTree or AggregatingMergeTree?

Use `SummingMergeTree` when every metric is a sum or count, and `AggregatingMergeTree` with `-State` and `-Merge` functions for anything else (distinct counts, quantiles, averages). In both cases the view aggregates each insert separately, so the target holds one partial row per key per insert until a background merge combines them. Always aggregate again when you read.

In a fresh `page_views_daily`, two inserts into `page_events` for the same day and page (two events, then one) left two rows in the target:

```sql
SELECT day, page, views FROM page_views_daily ORDER BY views;
```

```text
2026-11-08  /  1
2026-11-08  /  2
```

```sql
SELECT day, page, sum(views) AS views FROM page_views_daily GROUP BY day, page;
```

```text
2026-11-08  /  3
```

For an `AggregatingMergeTree` target, declare `AggregateFunction` columns, write them with `-State` functions in the view, and read them with the matching `-Merge` functions:

```sql
CREATE TABLE page_stats_daily
(
    day Date,
    page String,
    views AggregateFunction(count),
    users AggregateFunction(uniq, UInt32),
    p95_ms AggregateFunction(quantile(0.95), UInt32)
)
ENGINE = AggregatingMergeTree
ORDER BY (day, page);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW page_stats_daily_mv
TO page_stats_daily
AS SELECT
    toDate(ts) AS day,
    page,
    countState() AS views,
    uniqState(user_id) AS users,
    quantileState(0.95)(duration_ms) AS p95_ms
FROM page_events
WHERE ts >= '2026-11-09 00:00:00'
GROUP BY day, page;

SELECT
    day,
    page,
    countMerge(views) AS views,
    uniqMerge(users) AS users,
    round(quantileMerge(0.95)(p95_ms)) AS p95_ms
FROM page_stats_daily
GROUP BY day, page
ORDER BY day, page;
```

The backfill for this target must insert states too. Inserting a plain `count()` into an `AggregateFunction(count)` column fails with `Code: 70 ... Conversion from UInt64 to AggregateFunction(count) is not supported`. With the `-State` functions in the backfill `SELECT`, the same eight events as in the backfill section, and the backfill run one day at a time for 6, 7 and 8 November, the query above returned:

```text
2026-11-06  /         2  2  329
2026-11-07  /pricing  1  1  90
2026-11-08  /         2  2  194
2026-11-08  /pricing  1  1  75
2026-11-09  /         1  1  150
2026-11-09  /pricing  1  1  400
```

`countMerge(views)` over the whole target was 8, matching `count()` on `page_events`.

`countMerge` and `uniqMerge` return `UInt64`, and `quantileMerge` returns `Float64`.

## How do you alter or replace a materialized view?

To change the `SELECT` of a view that writes `TO` a table, use `ALTER TABLE view_name MODIFY QUERY`. To swap the whole definition in one statement, use `CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW`. Neither touches rows already in the target.

Adding a metric means changing the target first, then the view. Continuing from the two-insert example above (three events for `/` on 2026-11-08):

```sql
ALTER TABLE page_views_daily ADD COLUMN total_ms UInt64;

ALTER TABLE page_views_daily_mv MODIFY QUERY
SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views, sum(duration_ms) AS total_ms
FROM page_events
GROUP BY day, page;

INSERT INTO page_events VALUES ('2026-11-08 11:00:00', 3, '/', 200);

SELECT day, page, sum(views) AS views, sum(total_ms) AS total_ms
FROM page_views_daily
GROUP BY day, page;
```

```text
2026-11-08  /  4  200
```

`views` covers all four events, but `total_ms` only covers the one inserted after the change: older rows got the column default, 0. If the old values matter, the new column needs its own backfill. On 26.6, `MODIFY QUERY` worked without changing any setting (`allow_experimental_alter_materialized_view_structure` is 1 and marked obsolete). The [ALTER VIEW reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/alter/view) notes that it does not change the target table's structure, which is why the `ADD COLUMN` comes first.

`CREATE OR REPLACE` replaces the definition in one step:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW page_views_daily_mv
TO page_views_daily
AS SELECT toDate(ts) AS day, page, count() AS views
FROM page_events
WHERE page != '/health'
GROUP BY day, page;
```

Per the CREATE VIEW reference, `CREATE OR REPLACE MATERIALIZED VIEW` atomically replaces the view, and for a view without `TO` the old inner table is dropped and a new one created. With `TO`, only the definition changes and the target keeps its rows. `OR REPLACE` cannot be combined with `IF NOT EXISTS`.

## How do you show, list and drop materialized views?

Materialized views appear in `SHOW TABLES` alongside ordinary tables; there is no `SHOW MATERIALIZED VIEWS` statement (it is a syntax error on 26.6). To list only views, filter `system.tables` by engine:

```sql
SELECT name, as_select
FROM system.tables
WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND engine = 'MaterializedView';
```

To find which views fire on inserts into a table, read the source table's `dependencies_table` column. With two views reading from `src`:

```sql
SELECT name, dependencies_table FROM system.tables WHERE name = 'src';
```

```text
src  ['mv2','mv1']
```

`SHOW CREATE TABLE page_views_daily_mv` and `SHOW CREATE VIEW page_views_daily_mv` both print the full definition, including the `TO` target and the column list.

To drop a view, use `DROP VIEW` (or `DROP TABLE`, which also works on views):

```sql
DROP VIEW IF EXISTS page_views_daily_mv;
```

With a `TO` target, `page_views_daily` and its rows were still there afterwards. Inserts into `page_events` stop flowing to it from that moment, so recreate the view (and backfill the gap) if you only meant to change it.

## Creating a materialized view ON CLUSTER

The CREATE VIEW syntax accepts `ON CLUSTER`: `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW [IF NOT EXISTS] [db.]table_name [ON CLUSTER cluster_name] [TO [db.]name] ...`. Per the [distributed DDL docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/distributed-ddl), `ON CLUSTER` runs the `CREATE`, `DROP`, `ALTER` or `RENAME` on every host in the named cluster, and needs the same cluster definition on every host plus a connection to ZooKeeper or Keeper. Without it, the statement only affects the server you run it on. The CREATE VIEW reference also warns that `POPULATE` can miss or duplicate rows inserted through `ON CLUSTER`, a Distributed table or other replicas. I could not test a cluster for this guide, so check the details against those two pages for your setup.

## Querying the target table from TypeScript

Read from the target table, not the view, and aggregate again. With hypequery and a schema generated from your database:

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './schema';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  host: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_HOST!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

// { day: string; page: string; views: string }[]
const rows = await db
  .table('page_views_daily')
  .select(['day', 'page'])
  .sum('views', 'views')
  .where('day', 'gte', '2026-11-01')
  .groupBy(['day', 'page'])
  .orderBy('day', 'DESC')
  .execute();
```

`sum()` of a `UInt64` column is `UInt64`, so `views` arrives as a string, and `day` (a `Date`) does too. The `.sum(...).groupBy(...)` is the same re-aggregation as the SQL above, so the result does not depend on whether merges have run.

## Related

- [A guide to materialized views in ClickHouse](/blog/a-guide-to-materialized-views-in-clickhouse)
- [ClickHouse refreshable materialized views](/blog/clickhouse-refreshable-materialized-views)
- [FINAL vs ReplacingMergeTree dedup](/blog/clickhouse-final-replacingmergetree-typescript)
- [Type-safe schema management for ClickHouse](/blog/type-safe-schema-management-clickhouse)
- [ClickHouse time-series analytics](/clickhouse-time-series)
- ClickHouse docs: [CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/create/view), [Backfilling data](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/clickhouse/data-modelling/backfilling), [ALTER VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/alter/view), [Distributed DDL](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/distributed-ddl), [AggregatingMergeTree](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/aggregatingmergetree), [ClickHouse 26.8 release](https://clickhouse.com/blog/clickhouse-release-26-08)

posts.title: ClickHouse DateTime vs DateTime64: Date Types, Precision and Time Zones
posts.description: How ClickHouse's Date, Date32, DateTime and DateTime64 types store values, how column time zones change what you insert and read, and how to parse the results safely in TypeScript.
posts.body:
ClickHouse has four date and time types: `Date` and `Date32` store a calendar day, `DateTime` stores a Unix timestamp with one-second resolution, and `DateTime64(p)` stores ticks of 10^-p seconds, from `p = 0` up to nanoseconds at `p = 9`. Every `DateTime` and `DateTime64` value is a UTC instant; the time zone in `DateTime('UTC')` is column metadata that decides how strings are parsed on the way in and how values are printed on the way out. Over JSON all four types come back as strings without a time zone offset, so a TypeScript client has to know which zone the string was rendered in before it turns it into a `Date`.

Everything below was run on ClickHouse 26.6. For the bucketing functions (`toStartOfDay`, `toStartOfWeek`, `toStartOfInterval`) see [ClickHouse date functions in TypeScript](/blog/clickhouse-date-functions-typescript); this post is about the types underneath them.

## What are the ClickHouse date types?

ClickHouse's date types differ in resolution, range and size: `Date` and `Date32` hold days, `DateTime` holds seconds, and `DateTime64(p)` holds fractions of a second.

| Type | Bytes | Range on 26.6 | Resolution | Time zone |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Date` | 2 | 1970-01-01 to 2149-06-06 | 1 day | none |
| `Date32` | 4 | 1900-01-01 to 2299-12-31 | 1 day | none |
| `DateTime` | 4 | 1970-01-01 00:00:00 to 2106-02-07 06:28:15 UTC | 1 second | optional |
| `DateTime64(3)` | 8 | 1900-01-01 to 2299-12-31 | 1 millisecond | optional |
| `DateTime64(9)` | 8 | up to 2262-04-11 23:47:16 UTC | 1 nanosecond | optional |

```sql
SELECT
    byteSize(toDate('2026-03-01')) AS date_bytes,
    byteSize(toDate32('2026-03-01')) AS date32_bytes,
    byteSize(toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00')) AS datetime_bytes,
    byteSize(toDateTime64('2026-03-01 12:00:00', 9)) AS datetime64_bytes;
```

```text
2	4	4	8
```

Values outside the range are clamped without an error. Inserting `'2200-01-01'` into a `Date` column stores `2149-06-06`, and `'2200-01-01 00:00:00'` into a `DateTime('UTC')` column stores `2106-02-07 06:28:15`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE range_demo (d Date, dt DateTime('UTC')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY d;
INSERT INTO range_demo VALUES ('2200-01-01', '2200-01-01 00:00:00');
SELECT * FROM range_demo;
```

```text
2149-06-06	2106-02-07 06:28:15
```

`DateTime64(9)` is the exception: going past 2262-04-11 23:47:16 fails with `Decimal math overflow (DECIMAL_OVERFLOW)`. The current [DateTime64 docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/data-types/datetime64) describe a wider range than the one above, so if you rely on dates before 1900 or after 2299, check them on your own server version.

## Is ClickHouse DateTime precision seconds only?

Yes, `DateTime` has a resolution of one second, and any fractional part is truncated rather than rounded. Use `DateTime64(3)` for milliseconds, `DateTime64(6)` for microseconds or `DateTime64(9)` for nanoseconds; precision accepts 0 to 9, and 10 fails with `Scale 10 is too large for DateTime64`.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
CREATE TABLE precision_demo (dt DateTime, dt3 DateTime64(3), dt6 DateTime64(6))
ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY dt;
INSERT INTO precision_demo VALUES
    ('2026-03-01 12:00:00.999999', '2026-03-01 12:00:00.999999', '2026-03-01 12:00:00.999999');
SELECT * FROM precision_demo;
```

```text
2026-03-01 12:00:00	2026-03-01 12:00:00.999	2026-03-01 12:00:00.999999
```

`.999999` became `12:00:00` and `.999`, never `12:00:01`. The same happens with `toDateTime(now64())` or when a `DateTime64` value passes through a function that returns `DateTime`, such as `toStartOfDay`.

## How do time zones work in a ClickHouse DateTime column?

A `DateTime` column always stores seconds since the Unix epoch in UTC. The [DateTime docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/data-types/datetime) say the time zone "is not stored in the rows of the table (or in resultset), but is stored in the column metadata". The zone matters at three points: when a string is parsed into the column, when the value is printed, and when calendar functions like `toDate` or `toStartOfDay` decide which day a timestamp falls on.

Insert the same string into three columns and you get three different instants:

```sql
CREATE TABLE tz_demo (
    ts_utc DateTime('UTC'),
    ts_ny DateTime('America/New_York'),
    ts_default DateTime
) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY ts_utc;
INSERT INTO tz_demo SETTINGS session_timezone = 'Europe/Madrid'
VALUES ('2026-03-01 12:00:00', '2026-03-01 12:00:00', '2026-03-01 12:00:00');
SELECT toUnixTimestamp(ts_utc), toUnixTimestamp(ts_ny), toUnixTimestamp(ts_default) FROM tz_demo;
```

```text
1772366400	1772384400	1772362800
```

The string was read as noon UTC, noon New York (UTC-5) and noon Madrid (UTC+1). A column declared as plain `DateTime` uses the session time zone, which is the server's `timezone` setting unless the query or session sets `session_timezone`. That means the same stored row prints differently depending on who reads it:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events_plain (id UInt32, created_at DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;
INSERT INTO events_plain SETTINGS session_timezone = 'UTC' VALUES (1, '2026-03-01 12:00:00');
SELECT created_at, toUnixTimestamp(created_at) FROM events_plain SETTINGS session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT created_at, toUnixTimestamp(created_at) FROM events_plain SETTINGS session_timezone = 'Asia/Tokyo';
```

```text
2026-03-01 12:00:00	1772366400
2026-03-01 21:00:00	1772366400
```

`SELECT timezone(), serverTimezone()` shows both zones for the current session. If you declare event columns as `DateTime('UTC')` or `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')`, no server or session setting can shift them.

`toTimeZone` changes only the display zone. The instant and equality are unchanged:

```sql
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00', 'UTC') AS utc,
    toTimeZone(utc, 'America/New_York') AS ny,
    toTypeName(ny) AS ny_type,
    utc = ny AS same_instant
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
utc:          2026-03-01 12:00:00
ny:           2026-03-01 07:00:00
ny_type:      DateTime('America/New_York')
same_instant: 1
```

## How do you convert to DateTime in ClickHouse?

Use `toDateTime(value, [tz])` for strings, Unix seconds and `Date` values, `toDateTime64(value, precision, [tz])` when you need fractions, and `parseDateTimeBestEffort` for formats other than `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00', 'America/New_York') AS from_string,
    toDateTime(1772366400) AS from_seconds,
    toDateTime(toDate('2026-03-01')) AS from_date,
    toDateTime64('2026-03-01 12:00:00.123', 3, 'UTC') AS with_millis,
    toDateTimeOrNull('not a date') AS bad_input
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
from_string:  2026-03-01 12:00:00
from_seconds: 2026-03-01 12:00:00
from_date:    2026-03-01 00:00:00
with_millis:  2026-03-01 12:00:00.123
bad_input:    ᴺᵁᴸᴸ
```

A string without an offset is read in the zone you pass, or the session zone if you pass none. ISO 8601 strings with `Z` or `+02:00` keep their offset:

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    parseDateTimeBestEffort('2026-03-01T12:00:00Z') AS iso_z,
    parseDateTimeBestEffort('2026-03-01T12:00:00+02:00') AS iso_offset,
    parseDateTime64BestEffort('2026-03-01T12:00:00.123Z', 3) AS iso_millis,
    parseDateTimeBestEffortUS('03/01/2026 12:00') AS us_format,
    parseDateTimeBestEffort('03/01/2026 12:00') AS day_first
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
iso_z:      2026-03-01 12:00:00
iso_offset: 2026-03-01 10:00:00
iso_millis: 2026-03-01 12:00:00.123
us_format:  2026-03-01 12:00:00
day_first:  2026-01-03 12:00:00
```

The last line is the one to watch: without the `US` suffix, `03/01/2026` is read as 3 January. Invalid input throws `CANNOT_PARSE_DATETIME`; use `parseDateTimeBestEffortOrNull` when the data is untrusted.

## How do fromUnixTimestamp64Milli and fromUnixTimestamp64Nano work?

`fromUnixTimestamp64Milli`, `fromUnixTimestamp64Micro` and `fromUnixTimestamp64Nano` turn an integer epoch value into `DateTime64(3)`, `DateTime64(6)` or `DateTime64(9)`, with an optional time zone. `toUnixTimestamp64Milli` and friends go the other way and return `Int64`.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    fromUnixTimestamp64Milli(1772366400123) AS ms,
    toTypeName(ms) AS ms_type,
    fromUnixTimestamp64Nano(1772366400123456789) AS ns,
    toTypeName(ns) AS ns_type,
    fromUnixTimestamp64Milli(1772366400123, 'Asia/Tokyo') AS ms_tokyo,
    toUnixTimestamp64Milli(ms) AS back_to_ms
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
ms:         2026-03-01 12:00:00.123
ms_type:    DateTime64(3)
ns:         2026-03-01 12:00:00.123456789
ns_type:    DateTime64(9)
ms_tokyo:   2026-03-01 21:00:00.123
back_to_ms: 1772366400123
```

Do not pass a JavaScript millisecond timestamp to `toDateTime`. `toDateTime(1772366400123, 'UTC')` returns `2106-02-07 06:28:15`, the clamped maximum, with no error.

## How do you convert a ClickHouse DateTime to a Date or a string?

`toDate(ts)` returns the calendar day in the column's time zone, `toDate(ts, 'Zone')` returns it in another zone, and `toString(ts, ['Zone'])` returns the text form as a `String`. For custom formats use [formatDateTime](/clickhouse/functions/format-date-time).

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 23:30:00', 'UTC') AS ts,
    toDate(ts) AS d_utc,
    toDate(ts, 'Asia/Tokyo') AS d_tokyo,
    toString(ts) AS s_utc,
    toString(ts, 'Asia/Tokyo') AS s_tokyo,
    formatDateTime(ts, '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%i:%SZ') AS iso
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
ts:      2026-03-01 23:30:00
d_utc:   2026-03-01
d_tokyo: 2026-03-02
s_utc:   2026-03-01 23:30:00
s_tokyo: 2026-03-02 08:30:00
iso:     2026-03-01T23:30:00Z
```

The same timestamp falls on 1 March in UTC and 2 March in Tokyo. If your dashboard shows "events per day" for users in one region, pass that region's zone to `toDate`. More on the function itself is on the [toDate reference page](/clickhouse/functions/to-date).

## What do now(), now64(), today() and yesterday() return?

`now()` returns `DateTime`, `now64(p)` returns `DateTime64(p)` with a default precision of 3, and `today()` and `yesterday()` return `Date`. All of them use the session time zone unless you pass one (`now64(9, 'Asia/Tokyo')` has type `DateTime64(9, 'Asia/Tokyo')`), so `today()` depends on where the session thinks it is:

```sql
SELECT today() SETTINGS session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT today() SETTINGS session_timezone = 'Pacific/Kiritimati';
```

Run at 15:31 UTC on 8 November 2026, the first query returned `2026-11-08` and the second `2026-11-09`. `today() - yesterday()` is `1`, an `Int32` count of days.

## How does INTERVAL arithmetic work on ClickHouse dates?

`INTERVAL n UNIT` has its own type (`INTERVAL 7 DAY` is `IntervalDay`) and adding it to a date or time returns a date or time. Month arithmetic clamps to the end of the month, and adding a sub-second interval to a `DateTime` promotes it to `DateTime64`.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toDate('2026-01-31') + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS end_of_month,
    toDate('2026-03-01') - INTERVAL 1 HOUR AS date_minus_hour,
    toTypeName(date_minus_hour) AS dmh_type,
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00') + INTERVAL 500 MILLISECOND AS plus_ms,
    toTypeName(plus_ms) AS plus_ms_type,
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00') + INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours' AS compound
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
end_of_month:    2026-02-28
date_minus_hour: 2026-02-28 23:00:00
dmh_type:        DateTime
plus_ms:         2026-03-01 12:00:00.500
plus_ms_type:    DateTime64(3)
compound:        2026-03-02 14:00:00
```

## What happens when you compare DateTime with DateTime64 or a string?

Comparing `DateTime` with `DateTime64` converts both to `DateTime64` and compares the full value, so `12:00:00` is less than `12:00:00.750`. Comparing either type with a string literal parses the string in the column's time zone, using the column's precision.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00') AS dt,
    toDateTime64('2026-03-01 12:00:00.750', 3) AS dt64,
    dt = dt64 AS eq,
    dt < dt64 AS lt,
    toTypeName([dt, dt64]) AS common_type,
    dt = '2026-03-01 12:00:00.750' AS dt_vs_string
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
dt:           2026-03-01 12:00:00
dt64:         2026-03-01 12:00:00.750
eq:           0
lt:           1
common_type:  Array(DateTime64(3))
dt_vs_string: 1
```

`dt_vs_string` is `1` because the literal was parsed as a `DateTime` and lost its `.750`. The time zone rule is easy to miss: on a `DateTime('America/New_York')` column, `ts = '2026-03-01 12:00:00'` means noon in New York. The [session_timezone docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/settings#session_timezone) note that a string compared with a column "inherits the type and time zone of the existing column", while `toDateTime('...')` without a zone uses the session zone.

There is one more trap on 26.6. When the column is part of the table's sorting key, ClickHouse converts the literal for index analysis using only the basic `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` format. ISO strings fail, and so do fractional seconds on a `DateTime` key:

```sql
CREATE TABLE keyed (ts DateTime('UTC')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY ts;
INSERT INTO keyed VALUES ('2026-03-01 12:00:00');
SELECT count() FROM keyed WHERE ts >= '2026-03-01 12:00:00';
SELECT count() FROM keyed WHERE ts >= parseDateTime64BestEffort('2026-03-01T12:00:00.000Z', 3);
```

Both return `1`. `WHERE ts >= '2026-03-01T12:00:00Z'` on the same table fails with `Cannot convert string '2026-03-01T12:00:00Z' to type DateTime('UTC'). (TYPE_MISMATCH)`, and the same query works on a column that isn't in `ORDER BY`. Wrapping the value in `parseDateTime64BestEffort` works on `DateTime` and `DateTime64` keys in any time zone, because the `Z` fixes the instant.

## Why do times shift when you insert strings?

A string inserted into a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` column without an offset is read in that column's time zone, so `'2026-03-01 12:00:00'` from a UTC service lands five hours late in a `DateTime('America/New_York')` column. Strings with `Z` or an offset keep their instant when the parser accepts them, and that depends on `date_time_input_format`.

On 26.6 the default is `best_effort`, which reads ISO 8601 such as `2026-03-01T12:00:00.000Z`. `system.settings_changes` records that the default changed from `basic` to `best_effort` in 26.5; under `basic`, ClickHouse "can parse only the basic `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` or `YYYY-MM-DD` format", and a JSON row with `"2026-03-01T12:00:00.000Z"` fails with `CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED`. Run `SELECT getSetting('date_time_input_format')` on your server before relying on either behaviour.

`Date` columns are stricter still. A JSONEachRow value of `"2026-03-01T12:00:00.789Z"` for a `Date` column fails to parse even with `best_effort`; send `"2026-03-01"`.

## How does DST affect toStartOfDay in ClickHouse?

`toStartOfDay(ts, 'Zone')` returns local midnight in that zone as a `DateTime`, and on a daylight saving change the local day is 23 or 25 hours long, so adding 86,400 seconds to midnight does not land on the next midnight. `INTERVAL 1 DAY` does.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toStartOfDay(toDateTime('2026-03-08 12:00:00', 'America/New_York')) AS day_start,
    day_start + INTERVAL 1 DAY AS next_day,
    day_start + 86400 AS plus_86400,
    dateDiff('second', day_start, next_day) AS seconds_in_day;
```

```text
2026-03-08 00:00:00	2026-03-09 00:00:00	2026-03-09 01:00:00	82800
```

The day boundary in UTC also moves. Here the New York day starts at 05:00 UTC before the change and 04:00 UTC after it:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (id UInt64, created_at DateTime64(3, 'UTC')) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY created_at;
INSERT INTO events VALUES
    (1, '2026-03-08 03:30:00.120'), (2, '2026-03-08 04:59:59.999'),
    (3, '2026-03-08 05:00:00.000'), (4, '2026-03-09 03:59:59.500');
SELECT toDate(created_at, 'America/New_York') AS ny_date, count() AS events
FROM events GROUP BY ny_date ORDER BY ny_date;
```

```text
2026-03-07	2
2026-03-08	2
```

Rows 3 and 4 are 23 hours apart and still fall on the same New York day. Local times that don't exist or happen twice are resolved by rule: `toDateTime('2026-03-08 02:30:00', 'America/New_York')` returns `01:30:00`, and for repeated times the docs say "ClickHouse always picks the earlier occurrence".

## How do ClickHouse dates come back over JSON?

In JSON output formats every date type is a string. `Date` is `YYYY-MM-DD`, `DateTime` is `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` in the column's or session's zone with no offset, and `DateTime64(p)` adds exactly `p` fractional digits.

```sql
SET session_timezone = 'UTC';
SELECT
    toDate('2026-03-01') AS d,
    toDateTime('2026-03-01 12:00:00', 'UTC') AS dt_utc,
    toTimeZone(dt_utc, 'America/New_York') AS dt_ny,
    toDateTime64('2026-03-01 12:00:00.123', 3, 'UTC') AS dt64_3,
    toDateTime64('2026-03-01 12:00:00.123456789', 9, 'UTC') AS dt64_9
FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"d":"2026-03-01","dt_utc":"2026-03-01 12:00:00","dt_ny":"2026-03-01 07:00:00","dt64_3":"2026-03-01 12:00:00.123","dt64_9":"2026-03-01 12:00:00.123456789"}
```

`dt_utc` and `dt_ny` are the same instant, and nothing in the JSON says so. The `date_time_output_format` setting changes this. With `iso`, ClickHouse prints UTC with a `Z` (`"2026-03-01T17:00:00.123Z"` for a New York `DateTime64(3)` value at noon local time), which JavaScript's `Date` parses correctly. With `unix_timestamp` you get quoted epoch strings like `"1772366400.123"`. `Date` values stay `"2026-03-01"` in both modes.

## How do you parse ClickHouse dates in TypeScript?

hypequery types `Date`, `Date32`, `DateTime` and `DateTime64` columns as `string`, because that is what arrives over JSON. The risk is `new Date('2026-03-01 12:00:00')`: in Node 22 that string is read in the process's local time zone, so it gives `12:00Z` with `TZ=UTC`, `20:00Z` in Los Angeles and `03:00Z` in Tokyo.

The fix is to make sure ClickHouse renders UTC, then parse with an explicit `Z`. Store timestamps as `DateTime64(3, 'UTC')`, or set the session zone on the connection so plain `DateTime` columns render in UTC too:

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder, rawAs } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './schema';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  host: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_HOST!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
  clickhouse_settings: { session_timezone: 'UTC' },
});

// '2026-03-01 12:00:00.123' -> Date at 12:00:00.123 UTC
export function fromClickHouseUtc(value: string): Date {
  return new Date(value.length === 10 ? `${value}T00:00:00Z` : `${value.replace(' ', 'T')}Z`);
}

// Date -> '2026-03-01 12:00:00' (DateTime) or '2026-03-01 12:00:00.123' (DateTime64(3))
export function toClickHouseUtc(d: Date, millis = false): string {
  return d.toISOString().replace('T', ' ').slice(0, millis ? 23 : 19);
}

const since = new Date(Date.now() - 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000);

const rows = await db
  .table('events')
  .select([rawAs<string, 'ny_date'>("toDate(created_at, 'America/New_York')", 'ny_date')])
  .count('id', 'events')
  .where('created_at', 'gte', toClickHouseUtc(since, true))
  .groupBy('ny_date')
  .orderBy('ny_date', 'ASC')
  .execute();
// rows: { ny_date: string; events: string }[]
```

A few rules keep this correct:

- Return day buckets as `toDate(created_at, 'Zone')`. A `Date` string has no time of day, so there is nothing to misread. `toStartOfDay(created_at, 'America/New_York')` returns local midnight as a `DateTime` string, and `fromClickHouseUtc` would read it as UTC midnight, five hours off.
- `events` is a string because `count()` returns `UInt64`, which hypequery asks ClickHouse to quote.
- The filter string is read in the column's zone, so `toClickHouseUtc` is only right for UTC columns. For a column in another zone, use `.where((expr) => expr.raw("created_at >= parseDateTime64BestEffort('2026-03-01T00:00:00Z', 3)"))`.
- JavaScript `Date` holds milliseconds. `fromClickHouseUtc('2026-03-01 12:00:00.123456789')` returns `.123`. If you need all nine digits, select `toUnixTimestamp64Nano(created_at)`, which arrives as a string (it is `Int64`), and use `BigInt`.
- If you'd rather not write a parser, `clickhouse_settings: { date_time_output_format: 'iso' }` makes every `DateTime` and `DateTime64` string end in `Z`, and `new Date(value)` is then safe.

For a fuller tour of the builder see [hypequery for ClickHouse in TypeScript](/clickhouse-typescript), and for building time-bucketed charts see [ClickHouse time-series queries](/clickhouse-time-series).

- [toStartOfInterval function reference](/clickhouse/functions/to-start-of-interval)
