posts.title: ClickHouse Settings for Application Backends: Readonly Users, 64-bit Integers and Query Limits
posts.description: The ClickHouse settings a Node.js or Python API should configure: readonly = 1 vs 2, output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers, cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close, and limits like max_execution_time. Every example was run on ClickHouse 26.6.
posts.body:
An application backend should query ClickHouse as a dedicated user with `readonly = 2`, query limits such as `max_execution_time` and `max_result_rows` in that user's settings profile, `cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close = 1`, and `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1` if the client is JavaScript. `readonly = 1` and `readonly = 2` both block writes and DDL; the difference is that `readonly = 1` also rejects any setting change that differs from the profile, including the integer quoting that JavaScript clients send. Since ClickHouse 25.8 the default for `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers` is `0`, so `Int64` values such as `count()` arrive as bare JSON numbers and lose precision above 2^53 in JavaScript.

All SQL below was run on ClickHouse 26.6 with `clickhouse local`, and the HTTP examples against `play.clickhouse.com`.

## Which ClickHouse settings matter for an API backend?

Six settings cover most of what an API in front of ClickHouse needs: one for permissions, one for JSON encoding, one for cancellation and three limits. Here are their defaults on 26.6, from `system.settings`:

```sql
SELECT name, value
FROM system.settings
WHERE name IN ('readonly', 'output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers',
  'cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close', 'max_execution_time',
  'max_result_rows', 'max_bytes_to_read')
ORDER BY name;
```

```text
cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close	0
max_bytes_to_read	0
max_execution_time	0
max_result_rows	0
output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers	0
readonly	0
```

| Setting | Default on 26.6 | Suggested for an API user |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `readonly` | `0` (no restrictions) | `2` |
| `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers` | `0` (unquoted) | `1` for JavaScript clients |
| `cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close` | `0` | `1` |
| `max_execution_time` | `0` (unlimited) | Your API timeout, in seconds |
| `max_result_rows` | `0` (unlimited) | The most rows one response should return |
| `max_bytes_to_read` | `0` (unlimited) | A ceiling on uncompressed bytes scanned |

A `0` on the limits means no limit. The `system.settings` description for `cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close` notes a Cloud default of `1`, so ClickHouse Cloud and self-hosted servers differ here.

## How do I create a ClickHouse readonly user?

Create a settings profile with `readonly = 2` and your limits, create the user with that profile, and grant `SELECT` on the databases the API reads:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE analytics;
CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE api_profile SETTINGS
  readonly = 2,
  max_execution_time = 10 MAX 30,
  max_result_rows = 100000,
  max_bytes_to_read = 10000000000,
  cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close = 1,
  output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1;
CREATE USER api_reader IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password BY 'change-me'
  SETTINGS PROFILE 'api_profile';
GRANT SELECT ON analytics.* TO api_reader;
SHOW GRANTS FOR api_reader;
```

```text
GRANT SELECT ON analytics.* TO api_reader
```

`readonly` stops writes. Grants decide which tables the user can read. You need both: a readonly user with `SELECT ON *.*` can still read every table on the server.

## What is the difference between readonly = 1 and readonly = 2?

`readonly = 1` allows read queries only, and rejects any attempt to change a setting to a value other than the one already in effect. `readonly = 2` allows read queries plus `SET`, `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE` and `RESTORE`, and lets the client change any setting except `readonly` itself. The [permissions docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/permissions-for-queries) list what each level allows; the `system.settings` description reads "1 - only read requests, as well as changing explicitly allowed settings. 2 - only read requests, as well as changing settings, except for the 'readonly' setting."

Here is each level tested with `SET readonly = ...` in `clickhouse local`:

```sql
SET readonly = 1;
SELECT 1 SETTINGS max_execution_time = 5;
```

```text
Code: 164. DB::Exception: Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_execution_time' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY) (version 26.6.2.20 (official build)). (READONLY)
```

```sql
SET readonly = 2;
SET max_execution_time = 5;
SELECT getSetting('max_execution_time');
```

```text
5
```

| Statement | `readonly = 1` | `readonly = 2` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SELECT` | Allowed | Allowed |
| `INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)` | Code 164, `Cannot execute query in readonly mode` | Code 164 |
| `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Memory` | Code 164 | Code 164 |
| `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE` | Code 164 | Allowed |
| `SET max_execution_time = 5` | Code 164, `Cannot modify 'max_execution_time'` | Allowed |
| `SELECT ... SETTINGS max_execution_time = 5` | Code 164 | Allowed |
| Setting a value equal to the current one | Allowed | Allowed |
| `SET readonly = 0` or `SET readonly = 1` | Code 164, `Cannot modify 'readonly'` | Code 164 |

The "equal to the current one" row is why some clients work against a `readonly = 1` user and others don't. `play.clickhouse.com`'s `play` user has `readonly = 1` and `max_execution_time = 60`. Passing `max_execution_time=60` on the URL succeeds; passing a different value fails:

```bash
curl 'https://play.clickhouse.com/?user=play&max_execution_time=60' \
  --data-binary 'SELECT 1 AS x FORMAT JSONEachRow'
# {"x":1}

curl 'https://play.clickhouse.com/?user=play' \
  --data-binary 'SET max_execution_time = 5'
# Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'max_execution_time' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY)
```

If you need `readonly = 1` but want one setting to stay adjustable, mark it `CHANGEABLE_IN_READONLY` in the profile. The [constraints docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/constraints-on-settings) say this lets users change the setting within its `MIN`/`MAX` range even when `readonly = 1`:

```sql
CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p1 SETTINGS readonly = 1, max_execution_time = 10 CHANGEABLE_IN_READONLY;
SET profile = 'p1';
SET max_execution_time = 5;
SELECT getSetting('max_execution_time');
```

```text
5
```

For most APIs `readonly = 2` with constraints is simpler: the client can tighten limits per query, and `MAX` stops it raising them past what you allow.

## Why does ClickHouse return 64-bit integers as strings in JSON?

ClickHouse quotes `Int64`, `UInt64` and wider integers in JSON output when `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1`, because JavaScript parses JSON numbers as doubles and cannot represent integers above 2^53 (9007199254740992) exactly. On 26.6 the default is `0`, so they come back unquoted:

```sql
SELECT toInt64(9007199254740993) AS n FORMAT JSONEachRow;
SELECT toInt64(9007199254740993) AS n SETTINGS output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"n":9007199254740993}
{"n":"9007199254740993"}
```

Parse both in Node.js and the unquoted one changes value without any error:

```js
JSON.parse('{"n":9007199254740993}').n;   // 9007199254740992
JSON.parse('{"n":"9007199254740993"}').n; // '9007199254740993'
BigInt('9007199254740993');               // 9007199254740993n
Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER;                  // 9007199254740991
```

The default changed in 25.8. `system.settings_changes` on 26.6 records it as `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers` going from `1` to `0` with the note "Disable quoting of the 64 bit integers in JSON by default". The setting's own description in `system.settings` still says "Such integers are enclosed in quotes by default", so trust the `value` column rather than the text. If your API returned strings for `count()` on an older server and numbers after an upgrade, this is why.

The setting covers every integer type of 64 bits or more. `count()` returns `UInt64` and integer `sum()` returns `Int64` or `UInt64`, so both are affected:

```sql
SELECT toInt128(9007199254740993) AS a, toUInt256(9007199254740993) AS b, toUInt32(5) AS c
SETTINGS output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"a":"9007199254740993","b":"9007199254740993","c":5}
```

Python's `json` module parses big integers exactly (`json.loads('{"n":9007199254740993}')["n"]` returns `9007199254740993`), so the quoting matters mostly for JavaScript and TypeScript clients.

## Should I quote decimals and floats in ClickHouse JSON output?

Quote decimals if they can exceed about 15 significant digits. `output_format_json_quote_decimals` is `0` by default on 26.6, and a large `Decimal128` then arrives as a JSON number that both JavaScript and Python's default `json.loads` round:

```sql
SELECT toDecimal128('12345678901234567890.12', 2) AS d FORMAT JSONEachRow;
SELECT toDecimal128('12345678901234567890.12', 2) AS d SETTINGS output_format_json_quote_decimals = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"d":12345678901234567890.12}
{"d":"12345678901234567890.12"}
```

In Node.js, `JSON.parse` turns the first into `12345678901234567000`. In Python, `json.loads` gives `1.2345678901234567e+19` unless you pass `parse_float=decimal.Decimal`. For money columns with a few digits, such as `toDecimal64(12.34, 2)`, the unquoted `12.34` is fine.

`output_format_json_quote_64bit_floats` also exists (default `0`) and quotes `Float64` values. Floats are already doubles, so most APIs leave it off. Note that `NaN` and `inf` come back as `null` unless `output_format_json_quote_denormals = 1`:

```sql
SELECT toFloat64(0.1) AS f, 1/0 AS inf, toFloat64(nan) AS n FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"f":0.1,"inf":null,"n":null}
```

## Why does my readonly user reject output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers?

A `readonly = 1` user rejects `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1` because it is a setting change, and `readonly = 1` refuses setting changes whose value differs from the profile. JavaScript clients that send it per query hit this error:

```bash
curl 'https://play.clickhouse.com/?user=play&output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers=1' \
  --data-binary 'SELECT toInt64(9007199254740993) AS n FORMAT JSONEachRow'
# Code: 164. DB::Exception: Cannot modify 'output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers' setting in readonly mode. (READONLY)
```

You have four ways out:

1. Switch the user to `readonly = 2`. The client can then send the setting.
2. Keep `readonly = 1` and put `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1` in the user's profile. A request that sends the same value is accepted; a request that sends `0` is then rejected.
3. Mark the setting `CHANGEABLE_IN_READONLY` in the profile.
4. Stop sending the setting and accept unquoted integers, with the precision loss above 2^53.

Option 2, checked in `clickhouse local`:

```sql
CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE p1 SETTINGS readonly = 1, output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1;
SET profile = 'p1';
SELECT toInt64(9007199254740993) AS n SETTINGS output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1 FORMAT JSONEachRow;
```

```text
{"n":"9007199254740993"}
```

## What does cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close do?

`cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close = 1` makes ClickHouse cancel a read-only HTTP query, such as a `SELECT`, when the client closes the connection without waiting for the response. That is the `system.settings` description on 26.6. Without it, the [HTTP interface docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/interfaces/http) say "Running requests don't stop automatically if the HTTP connection is lost."

For an API this matters when a user closes the browser tab, your server times out a request, or a load balancer drops the connection. With the default of `0` on self-hosted ClickHouse, the query keeps running and using CPU and memory until it finishes or hits `max_execution_time`. ClickHouse Cloud's default is `1`.

Set it in the profile rather than per query. A `readonly = 1` user can't set it per query unless the profile already has the same value.

## Which ClickHouse settings stop expensive API queries?

`max_execution_time`, `max_result_rows` and `max_bytes_to_read` cap a query's run time, result size and scan size. Each throws an error when exceeded:

```sql
SELECT count() FROM numbers_mt(1e12)
SETTINGS max_execution_time = 1, timeout_before_checking_execution_speed = 0;
```

```text
Code: 159. DB::Exception: Timeout exceeded: elapsed 1000.217 ms, maximum: 1000 ms. (TIMEOUT_EXCEEDED)
```

```sql
SELECT number FROM numbers(1000000) SETTINGS max_result_rows = 1000 FORMAT Null;
```

```text
Code: 396. DB::Exception: Limit for result exceeded, max rows: 1.00 thousand, current rows: 65.41 thousand. (TOO_MANY_ROWS_OR_BYTES)
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE e (id UInt64, s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;
INSERT INTO e SELECT number, toString(number) FROM numbers(1000000);
SELECT count() FROM e WHERE s LIKE '%9%' SETTINGS max_bytes_to_read = 1000000;
```

```text
Code: 307. DB::Exception: Limit for rows or bytes to read exceeded, max bytes: 976.56 KiB, current bytes: 2.74 MiB: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPool, algorithm: Thread). (TOO_MANY_BYTES)
```

The elapsed time and byte counts in these errors vary slightly between runs. Three details from the `system.settings` descriptions that affect how you set them:

- `max_execution_time` is projected from execution speed. ClickHouse starts estimating after `timeout_before_checking_execution_speed` (10 seconds by default) and stops a query whose estimated time exceeds the limit. The example sets that to `0` to use wall-clock time. The docs also note the timeout can't fire during merging of aggregation states or query analysis, so real run time can be higher than the limit.
- `max_result_rows` is checked per block. With `result_overflow_mode = 'break'` the query returns a partial result instead of an error, but the size is rounded up to a block: the query above with `'break'` returned 65,409 rows for a limit of 1,000. Use `LIMIT` for exact page sizes and treat `max_result_rows` as a backstop.
- `max_bytes_to_read` counts uncompressed bytes. `max_rows_to_read` is the row-count equivalent (error code 158, `TOO_MANY_ROWS`).

`max_memory_usage` (default `0`, unlimited, on self-hosted) is worth adding to the same profile.

## How do I set ClickHouse settings per user, per profile or per query?

ClickHouse applies settings at four levels, and the narrower level wins as long as the user is allowed to change it:

| Level | How | Who controls it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Settings profile | `CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE ... SETTINGS ...`, or `<profiles>` in `users.xml` | Admin |
| User | `CREATE USER ... SETTINGS ...` or `ALTER USER ... SETTINGS ...` | Admin |
| Session | `SET name = value` | Client, if `readonly` allows it |
| Query | `SELECT ... SETTINGS name = value`, or HTTP URL parameters | Client, if `readonly` allows it |

Put the guardrails in the profile, add per-user overrides with `ALTER USER`, and let the application tighten limits per query. To set a user-level override on top of the profile:

```sql
ALTER USER api_reader SETTINGS PROFILE 'api_profile', max_result_rows = 50000;
SHOW CREATE USER api_reader;
```

```text
CREATE USER api_reader IDENTIFIED WITH sha256_password SETTINGS PROFILE `api_profile`, max_result_rows = 50000
```

Constraints decide whether a client override is accepted. With `max_execution_time = 10 MAX 30` in the profile, a client can lower or raise the timeout up to 30 seconds and no further:

```sql
CREATE SETTINGS PROFILE api_profile SETTINGS readonly = 2, max_execution_time = 10 MAX 30;
SET profile = 'api_profile';
SET max_execution_time = 20;
SET max_execution_time = 60;
```

```text
Code: 452. DB::Exception: Setting max_execution_time shouldn't be greater than 30. (SETTING_CONSTRAINT_VIOLATION)
```

## How do I query ClickHouse over the HTTP API?

ClickHouse's HTTP API is the SQL query endpoint on port 8123 (by default): send the query as the POST body, or as the `query` URL parameter, and read the result in the format named by `FORMAT` or the `X-ClickHouse-Format` header. The "ClickHouse REST API" people search for is this endpoint: SQL over HTTP. The public demo endpoint at `play.clickhouse.com` works the same way:

```bash
curl -H 'X-ClickHouse-User: play' -H 'X-ClickHouse-Format: JSONEachRow' \
  'https://play.clickhouse.com/?' \
  --data-binary "SELECT currentUser() AS u, getSetting('readonly') AS r"
# {"u":"play","r":1}
```

Facts from the [HTTP interface docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/interfaces/http) that matter for a backend:

- Credentials go in HTTP Basic auth, the `user` and `password` URL parameters, or the `X-ClickHouse-User` and `X-ClickHouse-Key` headers. When people search for a "ClickHouse API key" on the HTTP interface, `X-ClickHouse-Key` is it, and it holds the user's password. The docs advise against URL-parameter credentials because proxies may log them.
- Any setting can be passed as a URL parameter for a single query, as in the `max_execution_time=60` example above.
- The default output format is `TabSeparated`. `X-ClickHouse-Format` overrides a `FORMAT` clause in the query.
- The [permissions docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/permissions-for-queries) say a request whose method is not `POST` runs with `readonly = 2` if the effective value would otherwise be `0`. Use `POST` for anything that writes.

On 2026-11-08, `play.clickhouse.com`'s `play` user ran ClickHouse 26.10 with `readonly = 1`, `max_execution_time = 60`, `max_result_rows = 1000000`, `max_bytes_to_read = 1000000000000` and `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 0`. It's a working example of the profile-level guardrails described above.

## How do I build an API layer on top of ClickHouse?

Put your own backend between clients and ClickHouse, and have it connect as a readonly user whose profile carries the limits above. Exposing ClickHouse's HTTP endpoint directly to browsers means every client holds database credentials and can send any SQL its grants allow. A backend lets you authenticate your own users, apply tenant filters, choose which queries exist, and pick the JSON encoding your clients need. The checklist:

1. A dedicated user with `readonly = 2` and `GRANT SELECT` on only the tables the API needs.
2. `max_execution_time`, `max_result_rows`, `max_bytes_to_read` and `max_memory_usage` in the profile, with `MAX` constraints.
3. `cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close = 1` so abandoned requests stop.
4. `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1` for JavaScript clients, and `output_format_json_quote_decimals = 1` if you have wide decimals.

The [ClickHouse API page](/clickhouse-api) covers serving typed endpoints from these queries.

## Using these settings from TypeScript and Python with hypequery

hypequery's TypeScript query builder, `@hypequery/clickhouse`, sends `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1` with every query by default, so `Int64` and wider values, including `count()` and integer `sum()`, arrive as exact strings and are typed as `string`:

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder, rawAs } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './schema';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  url: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_URL!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

const rows = await db
  .table('events')
  .select([rawAs<string, 'day'>('toStartOfDay(created_at)', 'day')])
  .count('id', 'events')
  .where((expr) => expr.raw('created_at >= now() - INTERVAL 1 DAY'))
  .groupBy('day')
  .settings({ max_execution_time: 5 })
  .execute();
// rows: { day: string; events: string }[]
```

The adapter only adds that setting when you haven't set `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers` yourself in `clickhouse_settings` or per query, so explicit settings win. With the user types from earlier:

- A `readonly = 2` user, or an unrestricted one, works without changes, and so does `.settings({...})`.
- A `readonly = 1` user works if its profile already sets `output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers = 1`.
- Any other `readonly = 1` user rejects the setting with code 164. hypequery turns that specific rejection into an error telling you to set `integerJsonEncoding: 'server-default'`. Other readonly errors pass through unchanged.

```ts
const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  url: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_URL!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD ?? '',
  integerJsonEncoding: 'server-default',
});
```

`'server-default'` leaves the setting out rather than sending `0`, and doesn't probe the server or retry. The server's own setting then decides, which on a default 26.6 server means 64-bit values come back as JSON numbers that can lose precision above 2^53 and won't match the generated `string` types. Fixing the profile keeps the safe default. Per-query `.settings({...})` on a `readonly = 1` user follow the same rule: rejected unless the value matches the profile. `execute()` also accepts an `abortSignal`; the server stops the query on a dropped connection only if `cancel_http_readonly_queries_on_client_close = 1`.

The Python package attaches `readonly = 1`, `max_execution_time`, `max_result_rows`, `max_result_bytes` and `max_threads` to every dataset query. For a `readonly = 2` user it leaves out only the `readonly` setting and keeps every limit; for a `readonly = 1` user you set the same limits in the profile. The [readonly users reference](/docs/reference/readonly-users) has the details for both languages.

## Related

- [Read-only ClickHouse users in hypequery](/docs/reference/readonly-users)
- [Building a ClickHouse API](/clickhouse-api)
- [ClickHouse with TypeScript](/clickhouse-typescript)
- [ClickHouse with Python](/clickhouse-python)
- [Multi-tenant analytics on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-multi-tenant-analytics)
- [ClickHouse pagination in TypeScript](/blog/clickhouse-pagination-typescript)
- ClickHouse docs: [Permissions for queries](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/permissions-for-queries), [Constraints on settings](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/constraints-on-settings), [HTTP interface](https://clickhouse.com/docs/interfaces/http), [Settings reference](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/settings/settings)

posts.seoDescription: readonly = 1 blocks writes and setting changes; readonly = 2 blocks writes but allows SET. Plus 64-bit integer quoting, query limits and HTTP cancellation.

posts.title: ClickHouse View vs Materialized View: CREATE VIEW, Parameterized Views and SQL SECURITY
posts.description: The kinds of views in ClickHouse and how they differ: normal views, parameterized views, incremental and refreshable materialized views, plus CREATE, REPLACE, ALTER, DROP and SQL SECURITY. Every query checked on ClickHouse 26.6.
posts.body:
A ClickHouse view (`CREATE VIEW`) stores only a `SELECT` statement and runs it as a subquery every time you read from it, so it holds no data and is always current. A materialized view (`CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW`) stores results in a table: an incremental materialized view runs its query on each block inserted into the source table, and a refreshable materialized view re-runs the whole query on a schedule. ClickHouse also has parameterized views, which are normal views with typed placeholders called like a table function, and every view can run with the privileges of its definer or of the caller through `SQL SECURITY`.

The examples below were run on ClickHouse 26.6. They use a database called `shop` and this table, with one event per minute from 2026-11-01:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE shop;
USE shop;

CREATE TABLE events
(
    event_time DateTime,
    user_id UInt32,
    event_type LowCardinality(String),
    revenue Decimal(10, 2)
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY event_time;

INSERT INTO events
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-11-01 00:00:00') + number * 60,
    number % 100,
    ['view', 'click', 'purchase'][number % 3 + 1],
    toDecimal64(number % 50, 2)
FROM numbers(100000);
```

## What kinds of views does ClickHouse have?

The four kinds of views you will use in ClickHouse are normal views, parameterized views, incremental materialized views and refreshable materialized views. Only the materialized kinds store data.

| Kind | Created with | Stores data | When the query runs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal view | `CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT ...` | No | Every time `v` is read |
| Parameterized view | `CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT ... WHERE x = {p:Type}` | No | Every time `v(p = ...)` is read |
| Incremental materialized view | `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TO t AS SELECT ...` | Yes, in `t` | On each insert into the source, over the inserted block |
| Refreshable materialized view | `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv REFRESH EVERY ... TO t AS SELECT ...` | Yes, in `t` | On the refresh schedule, over all data |

The docs also describe live views, marked "deprecated and will be removed in the future" ([CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view)). This guide skips them.

## How do you create a view in ClickHouse (CREATE VIEW)?

`CREATE VIEW name AS SELECT ...` saves the query under a name, and reading from the view runs that query. The docs put it plainly: "a normal view is nothing more than a saved query", used "as a subquery in the FROM clause" ([CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view)).

```sql
CREATE VIEW purchases AS
SELECT event_time, user_id, revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase';

SELECT count(), sum(revenue) FROM purchases;
```

```text
33333	816650
```

Because nothing is stored, a new row in `events` shows up in the view immediately:

```sql
INSERT INTO events VALUES ('2027-01-15 12:00:00', 7, 'purchase', 99);

SELECT count(), sum(revenue) FROM purchases;
```

```text
33334	816749
```

Filters you add when querying the view still reach the source table's primary key. This query on `purchases` filters on `event_time`, the sort key of `events`, and the plan reads 7 of 13 granules (output trimmed):

```sql
EXPLAIN indexes = 1
SELECT count() FROM purchases WHERE event_time >= '2026-12-10 00:00:00';
```

```text
ReadFromMergeTree (shop.events)
Indexes:
  PrimaryKey
    Keys:
      event_time
    Parts: 2/2
    Granules: 7/13
```

A normal view is read-only. Inserting into one fails:

```sql
INSERT INTO purchases VALUES (now(), 1, 10);
```

```text
Code: 48. DB::Exception: Method write is not supported by storage View. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED)
```

`CREATE VIEW` on a name that already exists fails with `TABLE_ALREADY_EXISTS`. `CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS` does not fail, and it also does not change the existing view: in our test, the original definition stayed in place.

## How do you replace a view (CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW)?

`CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` swaps the stored query of an existing view, or creates the view if it does not exist. It is the way to change a normal view:

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW purchases AS
SELECT event_time, user_id, revenue, toDate(event_time) AS day
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase';

SELECT * FROM purchases ORDER BY event_time LIMIT 3;
```

```text
2026-11-01 00:02:00	2	2	2026-11-01
2026-11-01 00:05:00	5	5	2026-11-01
2026-11-01 00:08:00	8	8	2026-11-01
```

## Is there an ALTER VIEW in ClickHouse?

There is no `ALTER VIEW` statement, and normal views do not support `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY` either; on 26.6 both of these fail:

```sql
ALTER VIEW purchases MODIFY QUERY SELECT user_id FROM events;

ALTER TABLE purchases MODIFY QUERY SELECT user_id FROM events;
```

```text
Code: 62. DB::Exception: Syntax error: failed at position 12 (purchases): purchases MODIFY QUERY SELECT user_id FROM events;. ... (SYNTAX_ERROR)
Code: 48. DB::Exception: Alter of type 'MODIFY_QUERY' is not supported by storage View. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED)
```

For a normal view, use `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW`. For a materialized view, `ALTER TABLE mv MODIFY QUERY SELECT ...` changes the query and applies to future inserts only; the docs note that it "does not change the structure of the underlying storage table" ([ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/alter/view)). `ALTER TABLE v MODIFY SQL SECURITY` does work on a normal view, as shown below.

## How do you see a view's definition (SHOW CREATE VIEW)?

`SHOW CREATE VIEW name` returns the full `CREATE` statement, with the column list ClickHouse inferred and table names qualified with the database:

```sql
SHOW CREATE VIEW purchases;
```

```text
CREATE VIEW shop.purchases
(
    `event_time` DateTime,
    `user_id` UInt32,
    `revenue` Decimal(10, 2),
    `day` Date
)
AS SELECT
    event_time,
    user_id,
    revenue,
    toDate(event_time) AS day
FROM shop.events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
```

(`clickhouse local` prints this on one line with `\n` escapes; add `FORMAT TSVRaw` to get line breaks.) To list views, filter `system.tables` by engine; the `as_select` column holds the query:

```sql
SELECT name, engine
FROM system.tables
WHERE database = 'shop'
ORDER BY name;
```

```text
events	MergeTree
purchases	View
```

## How do you drop a view in ClickHouse?

`DROP VIEW name` (or `DROP VIEW IF EXISTS name`) removes a view; `DROP TABLE` on a view also works. `DROP VIEW` refuses to drop a real table, which makes it the safer statement:

```sql
DROP VIEW events;
```

```text
Code: 80. DB::Exception: Table shop.events is not a View. (INCORRECT_QUERY)
```

The reverse is not protected by default: with `check_referential_table_dependencies = 0` (the default on 26.6), `DROP TABLE events` succeeded while a view depended on it, and reading the view afterwards failed with `UNKNOWN_TABLE`.

## What is a parameterized view in ClickHouse?

A parameterized view is a normal view whose query contains typed placeholders such as `{event_type:String}`, and you pass values by calling the view like a table function: `view_name(event_type = 'purchase')`. It is useful for exposing one reusable query with a few inputs:

```sql
CREATE VIEW daily_by_type AS
SELECT toDate(event_time) AS day, count() AS events, sum(revenue) AS revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_type = {event_type:String}
  AND event_time >= {from:DateTime}
GROUP BY day;

SELECT *
FROM daily_by_type(event_type = 'purchase', from = '2026-12-01 00:00:00')
ORDER BY day
LIMIT 3;
```

```text
2026-12-01	480	11690
2026-12-02	480	11740
2026-12-03	480	11740
```

Reading it without arguments fails, because the docs note a parameterized view "doesn't have a schema when parameters are not provided" ([CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view)):

```sql
SELECT * FROM daily_by_type;
```

```text
Code: 51. DB::Exception: Empty list of columns in projection. In scope SELECT * FROM daily_by_type. (EMPTY_LIST_OF_COLUMNS_QUERIED)
```

In an application, pass the arguments as query parameters rather than building the string yourself. With `clickhouse local --param_t=purchase`, the query `SELECT * FROM daily_by_type(event_type = {t:String}, from = '2026-12-01 00:00:00')` resolved `{t:String}` before calling the view.

## What is a materialized view in ClickHouse?

A materialized view in ClickHouse is an insert trigger: when rows are inserted into the source table, it runs its `SELECT` over that inserted block and writes the result into a target table. The docs say materialized views "are implemented more like insert triggers", and any aggregation "is applied only to the batch of freshly inserted data" ([CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view)).

```sql
CREATE TABLE daily_revenue
(
    day Date,
    revenue Decimal(38, 2)
)
ENGINE = SummingMergeTree
ORDER BY day;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue_mv TO daily_revenue AS
SELECT toDate(event_time) AS day, sum(revenue) AS revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
GROUP BY day;

SELECT count() FROM daily_revenue;
```

```text
0
```

The 100,001 rows already in `events` are not in the target: the view only sees inserts that happen after it exists. A new insert flows through:

```sql
INSERT INTO events VALUES
    ('2027-02-01 08:00:00', 1, 'purchase', 100),
    ('2027-02-01 09:00:00', 2, 'purchase', 50),
    ('2027-02-01 09:30:00', 3, 'view', 0);

SELECT day, sum(revenue) FROM daily_revenue GROUP BY day;
```

```text
2027-02-01	150
```

Queries read `daily_revenue`, the target table, and use `sum()` because `SummingMergeTree` only combines rows when parts merge. Backfilling history, choosing the target engine and the `POPULATE` trap are covered in the [guide to materialized views in ClickHouse](/blog/a-guide-to-materialized-views-in-clickhouse).

## ClickHouse view vs materialized view: what is the difference?

A view costs nothing on insert and the full query on every read; a materialized view costs work on every insert and makes reads cheap, at the price of storing data and of never seeing updates or deletes on the source.

| | View | Materialized view (incremental) |
|---|---|---|
| Stores rows | No | Yes, in the target table |
| Work happens | At read time | At insert time |
| Freshness | Always current | Current as of the last insert |
| Existing source data | Included | Not included unless you backfill |
| `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` on source | Reflected | Not reflected |
| Change the query | `CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW` | `ALTER TABLE mv MODIFY QUERY` (future inserts only) |
| You query | The view | The target table (or the view name) |

Use a view to name and reuse a query, hide columns, or give users a stable interface. Use a materialized view when the same aggregation over a large, append-only table is too slow to run on every read. If the goal is a different sort order or a simple rollup of one table, a projection may fit better: see [projections vs materialized views](/blog/clickhouse-projections-vs-materialized-views).

## What is a refreshable materialized view?

A refreshable materialized view re-runs its full query on a schedule and, by default, atomically replaces the target table's contents with the result. It suits queries that incremental views handle badly, such as top-N lists or joins that should see all data:

```sql
CREATE TABLE top_users (user_id UInt32, revenue Decimal(38, 2))
ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY user_id;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW top_users_mv
REFRESH EVERY 1 HOUR
TO top_users AS
SELECT user_id, sum(revenue) AS revenue
FROM events
WHERE event_type = 'purchase'
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 3;

SYSTEM WAIT VIEW top_users_mv;

SELECT view, status FROM system.view_refreshes;
```

```text
top_users_mv	Scheduled
```

Without `APPEND`, refreshable views need an Atomic or Replicated database; in the default `Overlay` database of `clickhouse local`, 26.6 rejected the `CREATE` with `INCORRECT_QUERY`. Schedules, `DEPENDS ON`, `APPEND` and monitoring are in the [refreshable materialized views guide](/blog/clickhouse-refreshable-materialized-views).

## How does SQL SECURITY DEFINER work for ClickHouse views?

`SQL SECURITY DEFINER` makes the view's query run with the privileges of the user named in `DEFINER`, while `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` runs it with the privileges of whoever reads the view. `NONE` is the third value. In every case the reader still needs `SELECT` on the view itself ([CREATE VIEW, SQL security](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view)).

This test shows the view running as the definer. The session user (`default`) can read everything, but the view's definer can only read `events`, so the view fails:

```sql
CREATE USER report_owner IDENTIFIED WITH no_password;
GRANT SELECT ON shop.events TO report_owner;

CREATE TABLE salaries (user_id UInt32, salary UInt32)
ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY user_id;

CREATE VIEW salary_total
DEFINER = report_owner SQL SECURITY DEFINER
AS SELECT sum(salary) FROM salaries;

SELECT * FROM salary_total;
```

```text
Code: 497. DB::Exception: report_owner: Not enough privileges. To execute this query, it's necessary to have the grant SELECT ON shop.salaries. (ACCESS_DENIED)
```

The usual pattern is the opposite: a definer that can read the base tables, and readers that get `GRANT SELECT` on the view only. They can query the view without any grant on the tables behind it. Per the docs, setting a `DEFINER` other than yourself requires the `SET DEFINER` grant on that user.

To change it later:

```sql
ALTER TABLE salary_total MODIFY SQL SECURITY INVOKER;

SHOW CREATE VIEW salary_total;
```

```text
CREATE VIEW shop.salary_total
(
    `sum(salary)` UInt64
)
SQL SECURITY INVOKER
AS SELECT sum(salary)
FROM shop.salaries
```

What a view gets when you omit `SQL SECURITY` depends on the server setting `ignore_empty_sql_security_in_create_view_query`. On 26.6 it is `1`, and the docs say that then "the view gets an empty SQL security type"; a plain `CREATE VIEW` in our test showed no `SQL SECURITY` line in `SHOW CREATE`. With the setting at `0`, ClickHouse writes in the defaults: `INVOKER` for normal views (`default_normal_view_sql_security`), `DEFINER` for materialized views (`default_materialized_view_sql_security`), and `CURRENT_USER` as the definer (`default_view_definer`). Those three settings read `INVOKER`, `DEFINER` and `CURRENT_USER` on 26.6. Refreshable materialized views always get the defaults.

## Querying ClickHouse views from TypeScript

A normal view reads like a table, so a typed client can query it the same way. hypequery's type generator lists tables with `SHOW TABLES`, which returns views too, so `purchases` gets a generated type next to `events`:

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './schema';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  host: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_HOST!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

const topBuyers = await db
  .table('purchases')
  .select(['user_id'])
  .sum('revenue', 'revenue')
  .where('event_time', 'gte', '2026-12-01 00:00:00')
  .groupBy('user_id')
  .orderBy('revenue', 'DESC')
  .limit(5)
  .execute();
// topBuyers: { user_id: number; revenue: string }[]
```

`user_id` is `UInt32`, so it arrives as a `number`; the `sum()` result is typed as `string`. Pairing views with [read-only ClickHouse users](/docs/reference/readonly-users) is a simple way to give an app or an [MCP server](/clickhouse-mcp) a narrow, stable surface.

## Related

- [A guide to materialized views in ClickHouse](/blog/a-guide-to-materialized-views-in-clickhouse)
- [ClickHouse refreshable materialized views](/blog/clickhouse-refreshable-materialized-views)
- [ClickHouse projections vs materialized views](/blog/clickhouse-projections-vs-materialized-views)
- [Read-only users for hypequery](/docs/reference/readonly-users)
- [ClickHouse schema types in TypeScript](/clickhouse-schema)
- ClickHouse docs: [CREATE VIEW](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/create/view), [ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY QUERY](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/alter/view)

posts.seoDescription: A ClickHouse view stores only a query and runs it on every read. A materialized view stores results in a table, filled on insert or on a refresh schedule.

posts.title: Managed ClickHouse Services Compared: Which Platform Should You Use?
posts.description: Every active way to run ClickHouse without operating it yourself, checked on vendor pages: who runs it, where it runs, what ClickHouse you get, how it bills, and who each one suits.
posts.body:
Eight services let you run ClickHouse without operating it yourself, as checked on their own pages on 8 November 2026: ClickHouse Cloud, Tinybird, Altinity.Cloud, Aiven for ClickHouse, NetApp Instaclustr, Elestio, Alibaba Cloud ApsaraDB for ClickHouse and Yandex Managed Service for ClickHouse. DoubleCloud has wound down. For most developers the shortlist is ClickHouse Cloud (usage-based billing that scales to zero, run by the ClickHouse company), Tinybird (ClickHouse plus ingestion and hosted API endpoints, with a free plan), and Altinity.Cloud or Aiven (open-source ClickHouse on provisioned servers, with an option to run in your own cloud account).

## Managed ClickHouse services at a glance

Each row comes from the vendor's pricing page or docs, linked in the sections below.

| Service | Run by | Where it runs | What ClickHouse you get | Pricing model | Published entry point |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ClickHouse Cloud | ClickHouse, Inc. | Their cloud on AWS, Google Cloud, Azure; BYOC on all three | ClickHouse's cloud build on SharedMergeTree | Usage: compute-unit-hours plus storage | $300 credits for 30 days |
| Tinybird | Tinybird | Their cloud on AWS and Google Cloud | Native ClickHouse behind Tinybird data sources, pipes and endpoints | Plan sized in vCPUs plus overages | Free plan; Developer from $25/month |
| Altinity.Cloud | Altinity | Their cloud (AWS, GCP, Azure, Hetzner) or yours | Open-source ClickHouse, any version | Per server, vCPU and storage; BYOC per vCPU-hour | 14-day trial; BYOC from $0.0625 per vCPU-hour |
| Aiven for ClickHouse | Aiven | AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, DigitalOcean, OVH; BYOC on the first three | Open-source ClickHouse | Hourly rate per service plan | Developer tier $43/month |
| NetApp Instaclustr | NetApp | AWS and Azure (GCP coming), in their account or yours; on-premises | Open-source ClickHouse, version chosen at creation | Per node per month | Calculator on pricing page |
| Elestio | Elestio | 10 partner providers, or your own VM | Open-source ClickHouse on a dedicated VM | Hourly per service | From $11/month |
| Alibaba ApsaraDB for ClickHouse | Alibaba Cloud | Alibaba Cloud | Enterprise Edition (23.8) or Community-compatible (22.8 and older) | Subscription bundles | From $4,299.91/year |
| Yandex Managed Service for ClickHouse | Yandex Cloud | Yandex Cloud | ClickHouse servers on VMs | Per hour for host vCPU and RAM, plus storage | Price list for the Russia region |
| DoubleCloud | | Closed | | | Customers had until 1 March 2025 to move |

## ClickHouse Cloud

ClickHouse Cloud is the managed service run by ClickHouse, Inc., the company behind the open-source database, and it bills compute and storage separately by usage. Its [compatibility guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/guides/cloud-compatibility) says it is "based on the open-source ClickHouse distribution" with "a curated set of capabilities", and that MergeTree-family tables are automatically created as SharedMergeTree, an engine family that [powers ClickHouse Cloud](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/features/infrastructure/shared-merge-tree) on shared object storage.

- Deployment: ClickHouse's cloud on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with 38 region codes on the [supported regions page](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/reference/supported-regions), 21 of them public. [BYOC](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/guides/infrastructure/deployment-options/byoc/overview) is generally available on all three clouds but "requires customers to sign a committed contract", and BYOC doesn't yet include the SQL console, ClickPipes or autoscaling.
- Pricing: per the [pricing page](https://clickhouse.com/pricing), compute is metered per minute in compute units of 8 GiB RAM and 2 vCPUs. On AWS us-east-1 that is $0.2181 per unit-hour on Basic, $0.2985 on Scale and $0.3903 on Enterprise, plus $25.30 per TB-month of compressed storage. Idle services scale compute to zero.
- Limits: Basic tops out at 1 TB of storage and 8 to 12 GiB of memory in one availability zone. Scale adds two or more zones, private networking and compute-compute separation.
- Extras: ClickPipes for managed ingestion, [Query API endpoints](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/features/sql-console-features/query-endpoints) built from saved queries, and HTTPS, native and MySQL wire protocol access.

It suits teams that want the fewest operational decisions and an intermittent or growing workload where paying per compute minute helps.

## Tinybird

Tinybird is a data platform that runs ClickHouse underneath and adds ingestion, SQL-to-API endpoints, tokens and a branch-based development workflow. Its [managed ClickHouse page](https://www.tinybird.co/product/managed-clickhouse) says it "runs native ClickHouse under the hood", but you work through Tinybird resources, and its ClickHouse-compatible HTTP interface is [read-only](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/query-data/clickhouse-interface).

- Deployment: Tinybird's cloud, on shared infrastructure (Free, Developer, SaaS) or a dedicated cluster (Enterprise). The region lists in its docs cover AWS and Google Cloud. [Self-managed regions](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/core-concepts/self-managed) in your own account are in beta and meant for development only.
- Pricing: per the [plan docs](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/pricing) and [pricing page](https://www.tinybird.co/pricing), the Free plan has 0.25 vCPU, 1,000 requests a day and 10 GB with no time limit. Developer plans start at $25/month with 25 GB included, then $0.058/GB for storage and $0.0002 per second for vCPU overage. SaaS and Enterprise use credits with a 12-month commitment.
- Extras: Events API, Kafka, S3, GCS and DynamoDB connectors, a remote MCP server, TypeScript and Python SDKs, and Tinybird Local for development and CI.

It suits teams whose main deliverable is analytics APIs and who would rather not build ingestion or a serving layer. Our [ClickHouse Cloud vs Tinybird comparison](/compare/clickhouse-cloud-vs-tinybird) covers the trade-off in detail.

## Altinity.Cloud

Altinity.Cloud is a managed service from Altinity that runs unmodified open-source ClickHouse, either in Altinity's cloud or in your own account. Its [product page](https://altinity.com/managed-clickhouse/) says "We run 100% open source ClickHouse" and lets you "Run any version of ClickHouse". Altinity also maintains the open-source Altinity Kubernetes Operator for ClickHouse, which it says has been "downloaded over 100M times".

- Deployment: Altinity's cloud on AWS, GCP, Azure or Hetzner, or BYOC in your AWS, GCP, Azure, Hetzner, Nirvana or Kubernetes environment. Its [docs](https://docs.altinity.com/altinitycloud/) cover BYOC and BYOK (bring your own Kubernetes).
- Pricing: on the [pricing page](https://altinity.com/clickhouse-pricing/), hosted environments are billed hourly per server and per vCPU plus monthly per GB of storage, with rates shown in a region calculator. Up to $500/month of network costs per hosted environment is included. BYOC is per vCPU-hour: $0.0625 (Dev), $0.0833 (Enterprise) or $0.1111 (Premium), with storage free because you pay your cloud provider for it.
- Support: 24/7 support is included, also during the 14-day trial.
- Limits, in Altinity's own words: it "has limited built-in integrations", and it offers guided onboarding instead of a quick self-serve signup.

It suits teams that want open-source ClickHouse, hands-on support, or a managed service inside their own cloud account.

## Aiven for ClickHouse

Aiven for ClickHouse is a managed service "based on open source ClickHouse" ([docs](https://aiven.io/docs/products/clickhouse)) from Aiven, which also runs managed Kafka and PostgreSQL. Its pitch is a flat, predictable hourly price per plan.

- Deployment: the [ClickHouse pricing page](https://aiven.io/pricing/clickhouse) lists AWS, DigitalOcean, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure and OVH. [BYOC](https://aiven.io/docs/platform/concepts/byoc) is self-service on AWS, GCP and Azure but needs a commitment deal and the Advanced or Premium support tier.
- Pricing: you pay an hourly rate per service, invoiced monthly. The [product page](https://aiven.io/clickhouse) lists a Developer tier at $43/month (single node on DigitalOcean, 2 shared vCPUs, 4 GB RAM, 25 GB storage), Startup from $155/month and Business from $654/month. New accounts get $50 in credits. Aiven's free plans cover PostgreSQL, OpenSearch, Kafka and Valkey, not ClickHouse.
- Extras: a managed Kafka-to-ClickHouse connector, PostgreSQL integration, tiered storage, service forks and a 99.99% SLA.

It suits teams already on Aiven Kafka or PostgreSQL, or anyone who prefers a fixed plan price.

## NetApp Instaclustr

NetApp Instaclustr runs managed open-source ClickHouse clusters in its cloud account or yours. When you [create a cluster](https://www.instaclustr.com/support/documentation/clickhouse/getting-started-with-clickhouse/creating-a-clickhouse-cluster/) you pick the ClickHouse version, shard and replica counts, and the provider account: Instaclustr's (RIIA) or your own (BYOC).

- Deployment: "AWS and Azure are supported right now, with support for GCP coming soon", per the cluster docs. Instaclustr's [hosting page](https://www.instaclustr.com/platform/hosting-options/) also offers on-premises and hybrid setups.
- Pricing: the [pricing page](https://www.instaclustr.com/pricing/) quotes a price per node per month through a calculator. For BYOC, the price covers Instaclustr's management only, and you pay the cloud provider for VMs and storage. Partial node-hours are billed as full hours.
- Extras: console, API and Terraform provisioning, tiered storage, Kafka integration, AWS PrivateLink and an availability SLA of up to 99.99%.

It suits companies that already buy managed Kafka, Cassandra or PostgreSQL from Instaclustr, or that need on-premises support.

## Elestio

Elestio is a managed hosting platform that deploys open-source ClickHouse on a dedicated VM at a fixed monthly price. Its [ClickHouse page](https://elest.io/open-source/clickhouse) lists plans "starting at $11/mo" with backups, SSL, updates and monitoring included.

- Deployment: partner providers DigitalOcean, Amazon Lightsail, Linode, Vultr, Scaleway, Hetzner, Netcup, OVHcloud, Azure and T-Cloud, or "Bring Your Own VM" on other infrastructure.
- Pricing: hourly per deployed service, covering compute, storage, bandwidth and your support level, with no commitment.
- Limits: the Test support plan is email and forum only with no SLA; paid support plans add response-time guarantees.

It suits side projects that want a hosted server on a small budget.

## Alibaba Cloud ApsaraDB for ClickHouse

ApsaraDB for ClickHouse is Alibaba Cloud's managed service "built on the open-source ClickHouse project" ([overview](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/clickhouse/product-overview/what-is-apsaradb-for-clickhouse)), sold in two editions. The [edition comparison](https://www.alibabacloud.com/help/en/clickhouse/product-overview/comparison-between-the-enterprise-edition-and-community-compatible-edition) (last updated 1 April 2026) describes Enterprise Edition as serverless with compute-storage separation and SharedMergeTree on kernel 23.8, and Community-compatible Edition as ECS instances with cloud disks on versions 22.8, 21.8, 20.8, 20.3 and 19.15.

- Pricing: the [product page](https://www.alibabacloud.com/en/product/clickhouse) shows subscription bundles from $4,299.91 per year (single replica, 8+ cores, 2+ nodes) and $8,599.82 per year (double replica), both marked 15% off when checked.

It suits teams already on Alibaba Cloud, especially those integrating with OSS, MaxCompute or DataWorks. Check the kernel versions against the ClickHouse features you need.

## Yandex Managed Service for ClickHouse

Yandex Cloud's Managed Service for ClickHouse runs clusters of ClickHouse hosts on VMs, coordinated by ClickHouse Keeper or ZooKeeper. Yandex's site blocked automated reading when we checked, so these points come from the same pages in Yandex's [official docs repository](https://github.com/yandex-cloud/docs/tree/master/en/managed-clickhouse) ([pricing](https://yandex.cloud/en/docs/managed-clickhouse/pricing) on yandex.cloud).

- Pricing: host compute is charged per hour by allocated vCPU and RAM (including ZooKeeper hosts), plus storage, backups and internet egress, with a one-minute minimum billing unit. Ingress is free, and committed-volume discounts exist for vCPU and RAM. The published price list is for the Russia region.
- Limits: a single-host cluster is not highly available.

It suits teams already on Yandex Cloud.

## DoubleCloud

DoubleCloud no longer operates. Its site now shows "DoubleCloud has wound down operations", and its [final update](https://double.cloud/blog/posts/2024/10/doublecloud-final-update/) gave customers until 1 March 2025 to move to another platform.

## What is the best managed ClickHouse platform for developers?

For most developers the best managed ClickHouse platform is ClickHouse Cloud or Tinybird, and the deciding question is whether you want a database or an API platform. ClickHouse Cloud gives you full SQL from any client, usage billing and BYOC on three clouds. Tinybird gives you hosted endpoints, ingestion connectors, a local container and branches, and a free plan with no time limit. If you need open-source ClickHouse with no cloud-only engines, or managed ClickHouse in your own cloud account at a published per-vCPU rate, Altinity.Cloud is the main alternative.

## Which managed ClickHouse service fits a small budget?

The lowest published entry points are Elestio from $11/month, Tinybird's Free plan and Developer plans from $25/month, and Aiven's $43/month Developer tier. ClickHouse Cloud has no fixed entry price: after the $300 trial it bills per compute minute and storage, and idle services stop paying for compute, which keeps light, intermittent use cheap but makes the first query after an idle period slower. The cheap tiers have limits: Aiven's Developer tier is a single node, and Tinybird's Free plan caps you at 1,000 requests a day.

## Best managed ClickHouse for real-time event analytics at startup scale

For event analytics at startup scale, Tinybird and ClickHouse Cloud fit best: both include managed ingestion and both can start small, on Tinybird's Free or Developer plans or ClickHouse Cloud's usage billing. Tinybird has the Events API plus Kafka, S3, GCS and DynamoDB connectors and serves results as hosted endpoints, so a small team can go from events to an API without a backend. ClickHouse Cloud ingests through ClickPipes or any ClickHouse client. Avoid idling for customer-facing dashboards there, since ClickHouse's [idling docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/features/autoscaling/idling) don't recommend it for frequently used customer-facing features. For modelling the events themselves, see [real-time analytics on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-real-time-analytics).

## Altinity.Cloud alternatives and ClickHouse Cloud alternatives

The closest alternative to Altinity.Cloud is Aiven for ClickHouse or NetApp Instaclustr: all three run open-source ClickHouse on provisioned servers and offer BYOC. Aiven adds flat plan pricing and a self-serve Developer tier; Instaclustr adds on-premises support. ClickHouse Cloud is the alternative if usage billing and scale-to-zero matter more than open-source parity, and Altinity is the usual ClickHouse Cloud alternative for teams that want any ClickHouse version or published BYOC rates. If you are searching for an alternative to ClickHouse the database, every service on this page runs ClickHouse, so this list won't help you there.

## How to choose a managed ClickHouse service

Work through these in order; the first two usually narrow the list to one or two services.

1. Region and account. Check the region list for your cloud. If data must stay in your account, ClickHouse Cloud, Altinity, Aiven and Instaclustr offer BYOC, with conditions (committed contracts on ClickHouse Cloud and Aiven).
2. Database or platform. If services and BI tools need direct read and write SQL, rule out read-only access paths. If you want hosted endpoints, Tinybird or ClickHouse Cloud's Query API endpoints save you an API layer.
3. Billing shape. Usage billing (ClickHouse Cloud) suits spiky or intermittent load. Fixed plans or per-node pricing (Aiven, Instaclustr, Elestio, Tinybird Developer) suit steady load and fixed budgets.
4. ClickHouse version and features. Altinity runs any version, ClickHouse Cloud runs its own build with a curated feature set, and Alibaba's Community-compatible Edition is on 22.8 or older.
5. Exit path. Services that run open-source ClickHouse make moving to self-hosting simpler. Plan how you would export data before you commit.

## When is self-hosting ClickHouse reasonable?

Self-hosting open-source ClickHouse is reasonable when you already operate databases on VMs or Kubernetes, have someone on call for them, and either run a steady workload large enough that a managed service's margin matters or need control a managed service won't give you (air-gapped networks, specific versions, custom builds). ClickHouse is Apache-2.0 licensed and installs from the [official packages or Docker image](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/setup/self-managed/overview).

What you take on:

- Replication and coordination. Replicated tables need [ClickHouse Keeper](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/oss/deployment-and-scaling/keeper/index), which "replaces ZooKeeper and provides replication and coordination". The docs' [replication example](https://clickhouse.com/docs/guides/oss/deployment-and-scaling/examples/1-shard-2-replicas) uses five servers: two holding data and three coordinating.
- Backups, upgrades, monitoring and capacity planning, which the managed services above bundle in.

On Kubernetes, two Apache-2.0 operators do much of the work. The [Altinity Kubernetes Operator](https://github.com/Altinity/clickhouse-operator) handles cluster scaling with automatic schema propagation, version upgrades and Prometheus metrics. The official [ClickHouse Operator](https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-operator) manages ClickHouse and ClickHouse Keeper clusters through custom resources. There is also a middle ground: Altinity.Cloud's BYOK mode manages ClickHouse in your own Kubernetes cluster, and Altinity offers support for self-managed ClickHouse.

## A note on hypequery

hypequery is an open-source TypeScript and Python code layer that runs inside your application and doesn't host ClickHouse. It connects to any of the services above that accept standard ClickHouse connections, so changing hosts doesn't mean rewriting queries. See the [quick start](/docs/quick-start) or [ClickHouse with TypeScript](/clickhouse-typescript).

## Related

- [ClickHouse Cloud vs Tinybird](/compare/clickhouse-cloud-vs-tinybird)
- [ClickHouse with TypeScript](/clickhouse-typescript)
- [Real-time analytics on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-real-time-analytics)
- [Multi-tenant analytics on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-multi-tenant-analytics)
- [hypequery quick start](/docs/quick-start)
- [ClickHouse Cloud compatibility guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/guides/cloud-compatibility)
- [ClickHouse self-managed install](https://clickhouse.com/docs/get-started/setup/self-managed/overview)
