posts.title: ClickHouse Equivalents of Common Postgres and MySQL SQL
posts.description: A lookup table of ClickHouse equivalents for GROUP_CONCAT, string_agg, unnest, date_trunc, CASE, ILIKE, DISTINCT ON, percentile_cont, ON CONFLICT, UPDATE and more, with the outputs that differ from Postgres and MySQL. Every query was run on ClickHouse 26.6.
posts.body:
Most Postgres and MySQL analytics SQL runs on ClickHouse with small changes: `GROUP_CONCAT` and `string_agg` become `groupConcat(',')(x)`, `unnest` becomes `arrayJoin` or `ARRAY JOIN`, `CASE WHEN` works as written, and `date_trunc` exists but returns a `Date` for month and week. The changes that silently alter results are elsewhere: `7 / 2` returns `3.5` as `Float64`, `LIKE` is case-sensitive, `group_concat` with no delimiter joins with an empty string, and there is no `ON CONFLICT`, so upserts become `ReplacingMergeTree` plus `FINAL`. Every ClickHouse query on this page was run on ClickHouse 26.6.2.

## ClickHouse SQL equivalents table

The table maps the Postgres and MySQL form to the ClickHouse form. The sections after it show real output for the rows that behave differently.

| Task | Postgres | MySQL | ClickHouse | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Join strings in a group | `string_agg(s, ',')` | `GROUP_CONCAT(s)` | `groupConcat(',')(s)` or `arrayStringConcat(groupArray(s), ',')` | `string_agg` and `group_concat` are aliases; default delimiter is `''` |
| Collect values into an array | `array_agg(x)` | `JSON_ARRAYAGG(x)` | `groupArray(x)` | `array_agg` is an alias of `groupArray` |
| Array to rows | `unnest(arr)` | `JSON_TABLE(...)` | `arrayJoin(arr)` or `ARRAY JOIN arr` | `unnest` is an alias of `arrayJoin`; empty arrays drop the row |
| Truncate to month | `date_trunc('month', ts)` | `DATE_FORMAT(ts, '%Y-%m-01')` | `toStartOfMonth(ts)` or `date_trunc('month', ts)` | Returns `Date` |
| NULL fallback | `COALESCE(a, b)` | `IFNULL(a, b)` | `ifNull(a, b)` or `coalesce(a, b)` | Same semantics |
| Conditional | `CASE WHEN ... END` | `IF(c, a, b)` | `CASE`, `if(c, a, b)`, `multiIf(c1, a, c2, b, c)` | All three work |
| Conditional count | `count(*) FILTER (WHERE c)` | `SUM(c)` | `countIf(c)`, `sumIf(x, c)` | `FILTER (WHERE ...)` also works |
| String to array | `string_to_array(s, ',')` | none | `splitByChar(',', s)` | Separator comes first; `splitByString` for multi-char |
| Nth part of a string | `split_part(s, ',', 2)` | `SUBSTRING_INDEX(...)` | `splitByChar(',', s)[2]` | Arrays are 1-based; `[0]` returns `''` |
| Pagination | `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` | `LIMIT 20, 10` | Both forms | Same results |
| First row per group | `DISTINCT ON (k)` | `ROW_NUMBER()` subquery | `LIMIT 1 BY k` or `DISTINCT ON (k)` | Both respect `ORDER BY` |
| Case-insensitive match | `ILIKE` | `LIKE` (default collation) | `ILIKE` | `LIKE` is case-sensitive |
| Substring contains | `position('x' in s) > 0` | `LOCATE('x', s) > 0` | `position(s, 'x') > 0` or `s LIKE '%x%'` | Haystack comes first |
| Array contains | `'x' = ANY(arr)` | `JSON_CONTAINS(...)` | `has(arr, 'x')` | `hasAny`, `hasAll` for sets |
| Range filter | `BETWEEN a AND b` | `BETWEEN a AND b` | `BETWEEN a AND b` | Inclusive at both ends |
| Distinct count | `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` | `COUNT(DISTINCT x)` | `count(DISTINCT x)`, `uniqExact(x)`, `uniq(x)` | `uniq` is approximate |
| Median / percentile | `percentile_cont(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY x)` | none built in | `quantileExactInclusive(0.9)(x)` or `quantile(0.9)(x)` | `quantile` is approximate |
| Row number | `row_number() OVER (...)` | `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...)` | `row_number() OVER (...)` | Same |
| Previous row | `lag(x) OVER (...)` | `LAG(x) OVER (...)` | `lag(x)` or `lagInFrame(x)` | First row returns `0` for non-Nullable columns (Postgres: NULL) |
| Upsert | `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` | `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` | `ReplacingMergeTree` + plain `INSERT` + `FINAL` | No `ON CONFLICT` syntax |
| Update rows | `UPDATE t SET ...` | `UPDATE t SET ...` | `ALTER TABLE t UPDATE ...` or lightweight `UPDATE` | Lightweight `UPDATE` needs two table settings |
| Delete rows | `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...` | `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...` | `DELETE FROM t WHERE ...` or `ALTER TABLE t DELETE ...` | Rows are masked, removed at merge |
| Foreign keys | `REFERENCES` | `FOREIGN KEY` | none | Table-level `FOREIGN KEY` is accepted and dropped |
| JSON field | `data->>'plan'` | `data->>'$.plan'` | `JSONExtractString(data, 'plan')` or `data.plan` on a `JSON` column | No `->>` operator |
| Relative time | `now() - INTERVAL '7 days'` | `NOW() - INTERVAL 7 DAY` | `now() - INTERVAL 7 DAY` | Both interval forms parse |
| Integer division | `7 / 2` → `3` | `7 DIV 2` → `3` | `intDiv(7, 2)` or `7 DIV 2` | `7 / 2` → `3.5` (`Float64`) |

The examples below use this table.

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders
(
    id UInt32,
    customer String,
    status String,
    amount Float64,
    coupon Nullable(String),
    tags Array(String),
    created_at DateTime
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY id;

INSERT INTO orders VALUES
    (1, 'acme',      'paid',     120.5, 'FALL10', ['gift', 'rush'], '2026-11-01 09:15:00'),
    (2, 'acme',      'refunded', 40,    NULL,     ['rush'],         '2026-11-01 17:40:00'),
    (3, 'globex',    'paid',     99.99, NULL,     [],               '2026-11-02 08:05:00'),
    (4, 'globex',    'paid',     15,    '',       ['bulk'],         '2026-11-03 00:00:00'),
    (5, 'initech',   'pending',  60,    NULL,     ['gift', 'bulk'], '2026-11-03 23:59:59'),
    (6, 'Acme Corp', 'paid',     75,    NULL,     [],               '2026-11-04 10:00:00');
```

## What is the ClickHouse equivalent of GROUP_CONCAT?

The ClickHouse equivalent of MySQL `GROUP_CONCAT` and Postgres `string_agg` is `groupConcat(',')(column)`, or `arrayStringConcat(groupArray(column), ',')`. `group_concat` and `string_agg` are registered as aliases of `groupConcat`, and `array_agg` is an alias of `groupArray`.

```sql
SELECT
    customer,
    groupConcat(', ')(status) AS statuses,
    arrayStringConcat(groupArray(status), ', ') AS same_thing,
    groupArray(id) AS ids
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;
```

```text
Acme Corp   paid             paid             [6]
acme        paid, refunded   paid, refunded   [1,2]
globex      paid, paid       paid, paid       [3,4]
initech     pending          pending          [5]
```

The trap is the default delimiter. MySQL's `GROUP_CONCAT` defaults to a comma ([MySQL docs](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/aggregate-functions.html#function_group-concat)). ClickHouse's defaults to an empty string ([groupConcat docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/groupconcat)):

```sql
SELECT group_concat(status) AS no_delimiter FROM orders WHERE customer = 'globex';
```

```text
paidpaid
```

MySQL's `GROUP_CONCAT(x ORDER BY y SEPARATOR ',')` and Postgres's `string_agg(x, ',' ORDER BY y)` are both syntax errors in ClickHouse 26.6. To control the order, collect tuples, sort them, then join:

```sql
SELECT
    customer,
    arrayStringConcat(arrayMap(t -> t.2, arraySort(groupArray((created_at, status)))), ',') AS statuses_in_time_order
FROM orders
GROUP BY customer
ORDER BY customer;
```

More on `groupArray` variants is on the [groupArray reference](/clickhouse/functions/group-array).

## How do you explode an array into rows in ClickHouse?

Use `arrayJoin(arr)` in the `SELECT` list, or the `ARRAY JOIN` clause, to turn each array element into its own row. `unnest` is an alias of `arrayJoin` in 26.6, so Postgres `SELECT unnest(tags)` also runs.

```sql
SELECT id, arrayJoin(tags) AS tag FROM orders ORDER BY id, tag;
```

```text
1   gift
1   rush
2   rush
4   bulk
5   bulk
5   gift
```

Orders 3 and 6 have empty arrays and disappear. `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` keeps them with an empty string as the tag:

```sql
SELECT id, tag
FROM orders
LEFT ARRAY JOIN tags AS tag
ORDER BY id, tag;
```

```text
1   gift
1   rush
2   rush
3
4   bulk
5   bulk
5   gift
6
```

The [ARRAY JOIN guide](/blog/clickhouse-array-join-typescript) covers multiple arrays and joining arrays in parallel.

## How do you convert a string to an array in ClickHouse?

`splitByChar(',', s)` splits a string on a single-byte separator and returns `Array(String)`. Use `splitByString` for multi-character separators and `splitByRegexp` for patterns. The separator is the first argument, the reverse of Postgres `string_to_array(s, ',')`.

```sql
SELECT
    splitByChar(',', 'red,green,,blue') AS parts,
    splitByString(', ', 'red, green, blue') AS parts2,
    splitByChar(',', 'red,green,blue')[2] AS second,
    splitByChar(',', 'red,green,blue')[0] AS zeroth;
```

```text
['red','green','','blue']   ['red','green','blue']   green
```

Arrays are 1-indexed, and index `0` returns the type's default (an empty string here) instead of an error. `splitByChar(', ', s)` fails with `Illegal separator for function splitByChar. Must be exactly one byte`. Wrap the result in `arrayJoin` to get one row per part.

## Does ClickHouse have date_trunc?

Yes. ClickHouse has `date_trunc(unit, value)` (alias of `dateTrunc`, case-insensitive), alongside `toStartOfMonth`, `toStartOfDay`, `toStartOfHour` and `toStartOfInterval`. The return type depends on the unit: `year`, `quarter`, `month` and `week` return `Date`, while `day`, `hour`, `minute` and `second` return `DateTime` ([dateTrunc docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/functions/date-time-functions#date_trunc)).

```sql
SELECT
    date_trunc('month', toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00')) AS dt_month,
    toTypeName(dt_month) AS month_type,
    date_trunc('day', toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00')) AS dt_day,
    toTypeName(dt_day) AS day_type,
    date_trunc('week', toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00')) AS dt_week,
    toStartOfWeek(toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00')) AS start_of_week_mode0,
    toStartOfWeek(toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00'), 1) AS start_of_week_mode1
FORMAT Vertical;
```

```text
dt_month:            2026-11-01
month_type:          Date
dt_day:              2026-11-08 00:00:00
day_type:            DateTime
dt_week:             2026-11-02
start_of_week_mode0: 2026-11-08
start_of_week_mode1: 2026-11-02
```

2026-11-08 is a Sunday. `date_trunc('week', ...)` returned Monday 2026-11-02, the same as Postgres, but `toStartOfWeek` with its default mode returned the Sunday itself. Pass mode `1` (or use `toMonday`) when porting Postgres weekly reports. For buckets like 15 minutes, use `toStartOfInterval(ts, INTERVAL 15 MINUTE)`; see [toStartOfInterval](/clickhouse/functions/to-start-of-interval) and [toStartOfWeek](/clickhouse/functions/to-start-of-week).

`now()` returns `DateTime`, `now64(3)` returns `DateTime64(3)`, and `today()` returns `Date`. Both MySQL-style `INTERVAL 7 DAY` and Postgres-style `INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours'` parse:

```sql
SELECT
    toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00') - INTERVAL 7 DAY AS week_ago,
    toDateTime('2026-11-08 14:30:00') - INTERVAL '1 day 2 hours' AS pg_style,
    toDate('2026-01-31') + INTERVAL 1 MONTH AS month_end,
    dateDiff('day', toDate('2026-11-01'), toDate('2026-11-08')) AS days;
```

```text
2026-11-01 14:30:00   2026-11-07 12:30:00   2026-02-28   7
```

## How do you write CASE WHEN and IF in ClickHouse?

`CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` works unchanged in ClickHouse. `if(cond, then, else)` is the two-branch form (like MySQL `IF`), and `multiIf(c1, r1, c2, r2, else)` is the compact form of a multi-branch `CASE`. For conditional aggregates, use the `-If` combinators such as `countIf` and `sumIf`; Postgres `FILTER (WHERE ...)` also runs.

```sql
SELECT
    id,
    amount,
    CASE WHEN amount >= 100 THEN 'large' WHEN amount >= 50 THEN 'medium' ELSE 'small' END AS size_case,
    multiIf(amount >= 100, 'large', amount >= 50, 'medium', 'small') AS size_multiif,
    if(status = 'paid', amount, 0) AS paid_amount
FROM orders
ORDER BY id;

SELECT
    countIf(status = 'paid') AS paid_orders,
    sumIf(amount, status = 'paid') AS paid_revenue,
    count() FILTER (WHERE status = 'paid') AS paid_orders_filter
FROM orders;
```

```text
1   120.5   large    large    120.5
2   40      small    small    0
3   99.99   medium   medium   99.99
4   15      small    small    15
5   60      medium   medium   0
6   75      medium   medium   75

4   310.49   4
```

A `CASE` with no `ELSE` returns `Nullable` (`Nullable(String)` in our test), with NULL for unmatched rows. See [if](/clickhouse/functions/if), [multiIf](/clickhouse/functions/multi-if) and [sumIf](/clickhouse/functions/sum-if).

## How does ifNull work in ClickHouse?

`ifNull(x, fallback)` returns `fallback` when `x` is NULL, the same as MySQL `IFNULL`; `coalesce` takes any number of arguments, and `nullIf(x, y)` returns NULL when they are equal. An empty string is not NULL, so combine `nullIf` and `coalesce` to treat both as missing:

```sql
SELECT
    id,
    coupon,
    ifNull(coupon, 'none') AS with_ifnull,
    coalesce(nullIf(coupon, ''), 'none') AS empty_as_none
FROM orders
ORDER BY id;
```

```text
1   FALL10   FALL10   FALL10
2   \N       none     none
3   \N       none     none
4                     none
5   \N       none     none
6   \N       none     none
```

The result type of `ifNull(coupon, 'none')` is `String`, so the column is no longer `Nullable`. More on [coalesce](/clickhouse/functions/coalesce).

## Is ClickHouse LIKE case-sensitive?

Yes. ClickHouse `LIKE` and `NOT LIKE` are case-sensitive, and `ILIKE` / `NOT ILIKE` are the case-insensitive versions ([string search docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/functions/string-search-functions)). This matters when porting from MySQL, where `LIKE` is case-insensitive under the default `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci` collation ([MySQL docs](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/case-sensitivity.html)). `%` matches any run of characters, `_` matches one, and `\` escapes them.

```sql
SELECT
    customer,
    customer LIKE 'acme%' AS like_match,
    customer ILIKE 'acme%' AS ilike_match,
    customer NOT ILIKE 'acme%' AS not_ilike_match,
    position(customer, 'Corp') AS pos
FROM orders
WHERE id IN (1, 3, 6)
ORDER BY id;
```

```text
acme        1   1   0   0
globex      0   0   1   0
Acme Corp   0   1   0   6
```

For "contains" on a string, `position(haystack, needle)` returns the 1-based byte position or `0`, and `positionCaseInsensitive` ignores case. For "contains" on an array, use `has`:

```sql
SELECT id, tags, has(tags, 'gift') AS has_gift, hasAny(tags, ['gift', 'bulk']) AS any_of, hasAll(tags, ['gift', 'bulk']) AS all_of
FROM orders
ORDER BY id;
```

```text
1   ['gift','rush']   1   1   0
2   ['rush']          0   0   0
3   []                0   0   0
4   ['bulk']          0   1   0
5   ['gift','bulk']   1   1   1
6   []                0   0   0
```

## Is BETWEEN inclusive in ClickHouse?

Yes. ClickHouse docs define `a BETWEEN b AND c` as `a >= b AND a <= c`, so both ends are included ([operators docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/operators)). The surprise with timestamps is the upper bound: a date string compared with a `DateTime` becomes midnight, so the last day is cut off.

```sql
SELECT id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-03'
ORDER BY id;
```

```text
1   2026-11-01 09:15:00
2   2026-11-01 17:40:00
3   2026-11-02 08:05:00
4   2026-11-03 00:00:00
```

Order 4 at exactly `00:00:00` is included, which shows the bound is inclusive, but order 5 at `23:59:59` the same day is excluded. Filter on `toDate(created_at) BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-03'` or use a half-open range (`created_at >= '2026-11-01' AND created_at < '2026-11-04'`); both return all five November 1 to 3 orders. `3 BETWEEN 4 AND 2` returns `0`, so put the lower bound first.

## LIMIT, OFFSET and DISTINCT ON in ClickHouse

ClickHouse accepts `LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2`, MySQL's `LIMIT 2, 2` and `OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 2 ROWS ONLY`; all three returned ids 3 and 4. For deep pagination, keyset pagination scales better; see [ClickHouse pagination](/blog/clickhouse-pagination-typescript).

For Postgres `DISTINCT ON`, the ClickHouse idiom is `LIMIT n BY`, which keeps the first `n` rows per key after `ORDER BY`. ClickHouse 26.6 also accepts `DISTINCT ON`, and `EXPLAIN` shows it runs as the same `LimitBy` step after sorting:

```sql
SELECT customer, id, created_at
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer, created_at DESC
LIMIT 1 BY customer;
```

```text
Acme Corp   6   2026-11-04 10:00:00
acme        2   2026-11-01 17:40:00
globex      4   2026-11-03 00:00:00
initech     5   2026-11-03 23:59:59
```

`LIMIT 3 BY` gives top-3 per group, which `DISTINCT ON` cannot. The [LIMIT BY guide](/blog/clickhouse-limit-by-typescript) has more.

## COUNT(DISTINCT) and percentile_cont in ClickHouse

`count(DISTINCT x)` is exact by default in ClickHouse: it runs the function named by the `count_distinct_implementation` setting, which defaults to `uniqExact` ([count docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/count)). `uniq(x)` is approximate and uses an adaptive sample of up to 65,536 hashes ([uniq docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/uniq)).

```sql
SELECT
    count(DISTINCT number % 250000) AS count_distinct,
    uniqExact(number % 250000) AS exact,
    uniq(number % 250000) AS approx
FROM numbers(1000000);
```

```text
250000   250000   250699
```

For `percentile_cont`, `quantileExactInclusive(p)(x)` gave the same linearly interpolated answer as the `percentile_cont` formula in our test. `quantileExact` returns an actual value without interpolating, and `quantile` uses reservoir sampling (up to 8,192 values) and is non-deterministic on large inputs ([quantile docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/quantile)):

```sql
SELECT
    quantileExactInclusive(0.9)(x) AS like_percentile_cont,
    quantileExact(0.9)(x) AS quantile_exact,
    quantile(0.9)(x) AS approx
FROM (SELECT arrayJoin([1, 2, 10, 50]) AS x);
```

```text
38.00000000000001   50   38.00000000000001
```

With only four values the reservoir holds every value, so `quantile` matched the exact answer here. More in the [quantile reference](/clickhouse/functions/quantile).

## row_number, lag and lagInFrame in ClickHouse

`row_number()`, `lag(x, offset)` and `lead(x, offset)` work over the partition as in Postgres. `lagInFrame` and `leadInFrame` are ClickHouse extensions that respect the window frame, and the default frame ends at the current row ([window functions docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/window-functions)). So `leadInFrame` without an explicit frame always returns the default value:

```sql
SELECT
    id,
    amount,
    row_number() OVER (ORDER BY created_at) AS rn,
    lag(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at) AS prev_lag,
    leadInFrame(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at) AS next_default_frame,
    leadInFrame(amount) OVER (ORDER BY created_at ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS next_full_frame
FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at;
```

```text
1   120.5   1   0       0   40
2   40      2   120.5   0   99.99
3   99.99   3   40      0   15
4   15      4   99.99   0   60
5   60      5   15      0   75
6   75      6   60      0   0
```

The first `prev_lag` is `0`, where Postgres returns NULL, because `amount` is a non-Nullable `Float64`. Wrap the column to get NULL: `lag(toNullable(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY created_at)` returns `\N` on the first row. The [window functions guide](/blog/clickhouse-window-functions-typescript) covers running totals and frames.

## How do you upsert in ClickHouse without ON CONFLICT?

ClickHouse has no `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` or `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE`; in 26.6 both fail with `Cannot parse input`. The usual replacement is a `ReplacingMergeTree` table: insert the new version as a new row, and read with `FINAL` (or `argMax`) to get the latest version per sorting key.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users
(
    id UInt64,
    email String,
    plan String,
    updated_at DateTime
)
ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree(updated_at)
ORDER BY id;

INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ada@example.com', 'free', '2026-11-01 10:00:00');
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1, 'ada@example.com', 'pro', '2026-11-05 10:00:00');

SELECT count() AS rows_without_final FROM users;
SELECT * FROM users FINAL;
```

```text
2
1   ada@example.com   pro   2026-11-05 10:00:00
```

Deduplication happens only during background merges at an unknown time, and the docs state it "does not guarantee the absence of duplicates" ([ReplacingMergeTree docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/replacingmergetree)). `PRIMARY KEY` is not a uniqueness constraint either: inserting two rows with the same key into a plain `MergeTree` keeps both. See [FINAL and ReplacingMergeTree](/blog/clickhouse-final-replacingmergetree-typescript).

## UPDATE, DELETE and foreign keys in ClickHouse

ClickHouse has three ways to change rows. `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE` and `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE` are mutations: asynchronous by default and, per the docs, "a heavy operation not designed for frequent use" ([ALTER UPDATE docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/alter/update)). Lightweight `DELETE FROM` marks rows as deleted and merges remove them later ([DELETE docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/delete)). Lightweight `UPDATE ... SET` writes patch parts and requires the `enable_block_number_column` and `enable_block_offset_column` table settings ([UPDATE docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/update)).

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts
(
    id UInt64,
    plan String
)
ENGINE = MergeTree
ORDER BY id
SETTINGS enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1;

INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, 'free'), (2, 'free'), (3, 'pro');

ALTER TABLE accounts UPDATE plan = 'pro' WHERE id = 1 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET plan = 'team' WHERE id = 2;
DELETE FROM accounts WHERE id = 3;

SELECT * FROM accounts ORDER BY id;
```

```text
1   pro
2   team
```

Without those settings, `UPDATE` fails with `Lightweight updates are not supported` and suggests `MODIFY SETTING enable_block_number_column = 1`. The UPDATE docs recommend lightweight updates for changing about 10% of a table or less.

ClickHouse has no foreign keys. A table-level `FOREIGN KEY (customer_id) REFERENCES customers(id)` clause is accepted and dropped: `SHOW CREATE TABLE` no longer contains it, and inserting `customer_id = 999` with no matching customer succeeds. An inline `customer_id UInt64 REFERENCES customers(id)` is a syntax error. Enforce relationships in the application or check them with a `LEFT JOIN` ([joins guide](/blog/clickhouse-joins-typescript)).

## JSON operators in ClickHouse

ClickHouse has no `->` or `->>` operators. For JSON stored as `String`, use `JSONExtractString(json, 'key', 'nested_key')` and its typed siblings (`JSONExtractInt`, `JSONExtractFloat`, `JSONExtractRaw`), or `JSON_VALUE(json, '$.path')`. A missing key returns the type default, an empty string for `JSONExtractString`.

```sql
SELECT
    JSONExtractString('{"user": {"plan": "pro"}, "seats": 3}', 'user', 'plan') AS plan,
    JSONExtractInt('{"user": {"plan": "pro"}, "seats": 3}', 'seats') AS seats,
    JSONExtractString('{"seats": 3}', 'plan') AS missing,
    JSON_VALUE('{"user": {"plan": "pro"}}', '$.user.plan') AS json_value;
```

```text
pro   3         pro
```

With the `JSON` column type you use dot paths, and each path comes back as `Dynamic`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE events (id UInt32, props JSON) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id;

INSERT INTO events VALUES (1, '{"user": {"plan": "pro"}, "seats": 3}'), (2, '{"user": {"plan": "free"}}');

SELECT id, props.user.plan AS plan, toTypeName(plan) AS plan_type, props.seats AS seats
FROM events
WHERE props.user.plan = 'pro';
```

```text
1   pro   Dynamic   3
```

## Why does 7 / 2 return 3.5 in ClickHouse?

In ClickHouse, `/` returns `Float64` for integer and float arguments, so `7 / 2` is `3.5`. Postgres truncates integer division (`5 / 2` is `2`, per the [Postgres docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-math.html)). For integer division in ClickHouse use `intDiv(a, b)` or the `DIV` operator.

```sql
SELECT
    7 / 2 AS slash,
    toTypeName(7 / 2) AS slash_type,
    intDiv(7, 2) AS int_div,
    7 DIV 2 AS div_operator,
    intDiv(-7, 2) AS negative,
    7 % 2 AS modulo,
    1 / 0 AS by_zero,
    intDivOrZero(7, 0) AS int_div_or_zero;
```

```text
3.5   Float64   3   3   -3   1   inf   0
```

`intDiv(-7, 2)` returned `-3` on 26.6, truncating toward zero like Postgres. Division by zero with `/` returns `inf`, `intDiv(7, 0)` throws `Division by zero`, and `intDivOrZero` returns `0`.

The TypeScript side has the same split. `7 / 2` is `3.5` in JavaScript, `Math.trunc(7 / 2)` is `3` (and `Math.trunc(-7 / 2)` is `-3`, while `Math.floor` gives `-4`), and for 64-bit values `BigInt` division truncates: `7n / 2n` is `3n`.

## Using these from TypeScript with hypequery

In [hypequery](/clickhouse-query-builder), ClickHouse-only expressions go through `rawAs`, which also sets the TypeScript type of the result column. `countIf` returns `UInt64` and `intDiv(sum(amount), count())` returns `Int64` here, so both arrive as strings; `sum(amount) / count()` is `Float64` and arrives as a number. `DISTINCT ON` maps to `.limitBy()`.

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder, rawAs } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './schema';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  host: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_HOST!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

// GROUP_CONCAT, COUNT ... FILTER and integer division per customer
const perCustomer = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select([
    'customer',
    rawAs<string, 'statuses'>("groupConcat(', ')(status)", 'statuses'),
    rawAs<string, 'paid_orders'>("countIf(status = 'paid')", 'paid_orders'),
    rawAs<string, 'avg_whole'>('intDiv(sum(amount), count())', 'avg_whole'),
    rawAs<number, 'avg_amount'>('sum(amount) / count()', 'avg_amount'),
  ])
  .groupBy('customer')
  .orderBy('customer', 'ASC')
  .execute();

// DISTINCT ON (customer) ... ORDER BY customer, created_at DESC
const latestPerCustomer = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select(['customer', 'id', 'created_at'])
  .orderBy('customer', 'ASC')
  .orderBy('created_at', 'DESC')
  .limitBy(1, 'customer')
  .execute();

// Explode tags, with a date filter that keeps the whole last day
const tagRows = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select(['id', rawAs<string, 'tag'>('arrayJoin(tags)', 'tag')])
  .where((expr) => expr.raw("toDate(created_at) BETWEEN '2026-11-01' AND '2026-11-03'"))
  .execute();
```

Convert `paid_orders` with `Number()` when it fits in 53 bits, or `BigInt()` when it may not. The [quick start](/docs/quick-start) generates the `IntrospectedSchema` type from your tables.

## Related

- [ClickHouse date functions in TypeScript](/blog/clickhouse-date-functions-typescript)
- [ClickHouse ARRAY JOIN in TypeScript](/blog/clickhouse-array-join-typescript)
- [ClickHouse LIMIT BY](/blog/clickhouse-limit-by-typescript)
- [ClickHouse window functions in TypeScript](/blog/clickhouse-window-functions-typescript)
- [FINAL and ReplacingMergeTree](/blog/clickhouse-final-replacingmergetree-typescript)
- [ClickHouse query builder for TypeScript](/clickhouse-query-builder)
- ClickHouse docs: [groupConcat](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/aggregate-functions/reference/groupconcat), [dateTrunc](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/functions/date-time-functions#date_trunc), [operators](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/operators), [window functions](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/window-functions), [ReplacingMergeTree](https://clickhouse.com/docs/engines/table-engines/mergetree-family/replacingmergetree), [lightweight UPDATE](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/update), [lightweight DELETE](https://clickhouse.com/docs/sql-reference/statements/delete)

posts.title: Introducing hypequery for Python: A Semantic Layer for ClickHouse
posts.description: Define ClickHouse measures, dimensions, and tenant rules once in Python, query them by name, serve them from FastAPI, Django, or Flask, and use them from type-safe React hooks and AI agents.
posts.body:
Today we are launching the **hypequery for Python beta**: the same code-first semantic layer for ClickHouse that TypeScript teams use, now as a Python SDK.

You define datasets in Python: the dimensions people can group by, the measures they can aggregate, the relationships between tables, and the tenant rules every query must follow. Then you query those definitions by name from jobs, notebooks, and services, serve them over HTTP from the framework you already use (FastAPI, Django, Flask, or any ASGI or WSGI app) with authentication on by default, and use the same definitions from generated, type-safe React hooks and from AI agents over MCP.

```bash
pip install "hypequery[clickhouse]==0.1.0b2"
```

This is a beta (`0.1.0b2`): the APIs may still change before 1.0, so pin the version you deploy.

## Why Python

Plenty of ClickHouse analytics lives in Python: data pipelines, scheduled reports, notebooks, and FastAPI, Django, and Flask backends. Those teams hit the same problem TypeScript teams do. The definition of revenue is copied across services, each copy drifts, and in a multi-tenant product every query depends on someone remembering the tenant filter.

A driver like clickhouse-connect gets rows out of ClickHouse. It does not know what revenue means, which fields a caller may group by, or how to keep one customer's data away from another. That is the job of a semantic layer, and we think it belongs in your codebase rather than in YAML files or a separate server.

## Define a dataset

A dataset maps a ClickHouse table to named dimensions and measures. It is plain Python, validated when you create it, and reviewed in pull requests like the rest of your application.

```python
from hypequery.datasets import Dataset, dimension, measure

orders = Dataset(
    name="orders",
    source="orders",
    tenant_key="tenant_id",
    time_key="created_at",
    dimensions={
        "country": dimension("string"),
        "status": dimension("string"),
        "created_at": dimension("timestamp"),
    },
    measures={
        "revenue": measure.sum("amount"),
        "order_count": measure.count("id"),
    },
)
```

## Query it by name

Queries select semantic names. hypequery plans parameterized ClickHouse SQL and adds the tenant predicate from a trusted execution context, never from the query itself.

```python
from hypequery.datasets import DatasetQuery, ExecutionContext, create_dataset_client, filter, tenant
from hypequery.execution import ClickHouseConnection, create_clickhouse_executor

executor = create_clickhouse_executor(
    ClickHouseConnection(host="localhost", database="analytics")
)
analytics = create_dataset_client(executor=executor)

result = analytics.execute(
    orders,
    DatasetQuery(
        dimensions=("country",),
        measures=("revenue", "order_count"),
        filters=(filter.eq("status", "completed"),),
        by="month",
    ),
    context=ExecutionContext(tenant=tenant("org_123")),
)
```

A query against a tenant-scoped dataset without tenant context is rejected, and so is a filter that tries to set the tenant itself. The client also supports sync and async execution, result caching with tenant-safe keys, validation without execution, and to-one relationships with automatic joins.

## Serve it from your app

When a dashboard, a customer, or an integration needs the same numbers over HTTP, create an API, register the dataset as an endpoint, and mount it in the app you already run:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from hypequery.serve import (
    Credential,
    EndpointPolicy,
    HttpSecurity,
    Principal,
    add_dataset_endpoint,
    create_api,
    to_asgi_app,
)


async def authenticate(credential: Credential) -> Principal | None:
    claims = await verify_jwt(credential.value)  # your token verification
    if claims is None:
        return None
    return Principal(
        subject=claims["sub"],
        scopes=frozenset(claims.get("scope", "").split()),
        tenant_id=claims.get("org_id"),
    )


api = create_api(
    auth=authenticate,
    security=HttpSecurity(allowed_hosts=("analytics.example.com",)),
)
add_dataset_endpoint(
    api,
    "/datasets/orders/query",
    dataset=orders,
    client=analytics,
    policy=EndpointPolicy(required_scopes=frozenset({"analytics:read"}), tenant="required"),
)

app = FastAPI()  # your existing app and routes
app.mount("/analytics", to_asgi_app(api))
```

The API isn't tied to FastAPI. The same `api` mounts natively in Django with `path("analytics/", include(urls(api)))`, in Flask with `app.register_blueprint(blueprint(api), url_prefix="/analytics")`, under Starlette's `Mount`, or behind uvicorn or gunicorn with `to_asgi_app(api)` and `to_wsgi_app(api)`.

Every route requires authentication unless you mark it public, and authentication runs before the request body is read. Request bodies are validated strictly, so a caller cannot slip in SQL, an extra field, or a different tenant. Built in: JWT verification, roles and scopes per endpoint, rate limiting, CORS, trusted proxies, request ids, a discovery catalog, and a production profile. In Django and Flask apps, endpoints can also use your app's own login session, with a same-origin check, instead of a token.

## Django, Flask, and notebooks

You don't need HTTP to use the model. The Django and Flask integrations give every request a client already bound to the signed-in user's tenant, and results convert straight to DataFrames:

```python
# a Django view, with hypequery.contrib.django installed
def revenue_by_country(request):
    result = request.analytics.execute(
        "orders", {"dimensions": ["country"], "measures": ["revenue"]}
    )
    return JsonResponse({"data": list(result.data)})


# a notebook or a scheduled job
df = (
    analytics.for_tenant(tenant("org_123"))
    .execute("orders", {"measures": ["revenue"], "by": "month"})
    .to_pandas()
)
```

There is also an [SQLAlchemy helper](/clickhouse-sqlalchemy) that reuses your engine's ClickHouse connection, and `to_polars()` and `to_arrow()` alongside `to_pandas()`. For a walkthrough per framework, see [ClickHouse with Django](/clickhouse-django), [Flask](/clickhouse-flask), and [pandas](/clickhouse-pandas).

## Type-safe React hooks and AI agents

Install your endpoints with a `client_profile`, and your frontend can call them through the same `@hypequery/react` hooks TypeScript backends use, fully typed. It takes two steps: export a **client contract** from Python (a JSON file listing the fields, operators, and limits each endpoint accepts), then generate a typed client from it in your frontend ([full walkthrough](/fastapi-react-analytics)):

```bash
# In your Python project: export the contract
python -m hypequery export client-contract --factory analytics.definitions:build --output web/client-contract.json

# In your frontend: generate the typed client
npx hypequery generate:client client-contract.json
```

Here, `build` is a small function in your definitions module that lists the endpoints to publish. You commit the contract like any other file, and `--check` fails CI when the definitions change but the contract doesn't.

```tsx
const { data } = useDataset('orders', {
  dimensions: ['country'],
  measures: ['revenue'],
  filters: [{ field: 'status', operator: 'eq', value: 'completed' }],
});
// data.data rows are typed { country: string | null; revenue: string | null }
```

Misspell a field, filter a number with a string, or ask for a dimension the endpoint doesn't expose, and TypeScript stops the build. If the Python definitions change after the frontend is built, the server answers `409` instead of returning data in a shape the types don't describe.

The same endpoints serve AI agents. `hypequery mcp --client-contract-url` connects Claude, Cursor, or any MCP client to the authorized endpoints for one principal, so agents query the governed definitions, never raw SQL. See [ClickHouse MCP from Python](/clickhouse-python-mcp).

## One model, two languages

Python and TypeScript implement the same specifications and run against the same conformance fixtures. Equivalent definitions produce identical semantic and deployment artifacts, and the HTTP endpoints share one request format and response envelope, checked by shared fixtures in CI.

That means a team can define analytics in whichever language fits each service. A Python pipeline and a TypeScript API can rely on the same model without the two drifting apart.

## What's next

The Python SDK covers datasets, derived measures, relationships, execution, caching, multi-tenancy, serving from FastAPI, Django, Flask, or any ASGI or WSGI app, DataFrame output, and a CLI that scaffolds a project from your live schema today. Some newer dataset features are TypeScript-only for now, including window measures, period comparisons, segments, merge measures over `AggregatingMergeTree` state columns, and `final: true` reads. We are bringing them to Python next, and the [feature status page](/docs/python/feature-status) tracks where each one stands.

## Get started

- [Python quick start](/docs/python/quick-start): define a dataset and run your first query
- [Serve your datasets](/docs/python/serving): expose datasets as authenticated endpoints and mount them anywhere
- [Django](/docs/python/django), [Flask](/docs/python/flask), and [FastAPI](/docs/python/fastapi): framework guides
- [React and MCP clients](/docs/python/client-endpoints): typed React hooks and agent tools over the same endpoints
- [ClickHouse with Python](/clickhouse-python): how hypequery fits next to your driver
- [hypequery vs clickhouse-connect](/compare/hypequery-vs-clickhouse-connect): when to keep the driver, and when shared datasets earn their place
- [Python semantic layer](/python-semantic-layer) and [multi-tenant analytics in Python](/clickhouse-python-multi-tenant)

hypequery is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. If you try it, we would love to hear what you build.

posts.title: hypequery vs clickhouse-connect: Driver or Semantic Layer?
posts.description: clickhouse-connect runs the SQL you write. hypequery runs on top of it and adds shared measures, validation, and tenant isolation. Here is when you need each in Python.
posts.body:
clickhouse-connect is the official ClickHouse driver for Python. It sends SQL over HTTP, binds parameters on the server, and hands results back as Python values, NumPy arrays, pandas DataFrames, or Arrow tables. It also does fast bulk inserts. If you run ClickHouse from Python, you probably already use it.

hypequery is not a different driver. Its Python package runs on clickhouse-connect. What it adds sits above the driver: a definition of what your numbers mean, and rules about who may ask for them.

So this isn't really a choice between two tools. The question is whether your analytics SQL needs a layer on top.

## What clickhouse-connect gives you

- **Any SQL you can write.** Queries, DDL, inserts, settings, and system tables.
- **Server-side parameters.** Values are bound by ClickHouse, not interpolated into strings.
- **Data-science output.** `query_df` and `query_arrow` return DataFrames and Arrow tables directly.
- **Bulk inserts.** Columnar inserts and async inserts for ingestion.

It does not know what "revenue" means, which customer a request belongs to, or which fields a caller should be allowed to group by. That knowledge lives in your SQL strings.

## What hypequery adds

You describe a dataset once: its table, dimensions, measures, time column, and tenant key.

```python
from hypequery.datasets import Dataset, dimension, measure

orders = Dataset(
    name="orders",
    source="orders",
    tenant_key="org_id",
    time_key="created_at",
    dimensions={"status": dimension("string"), "country": dimension("string")},
    measures={"revenue": measure.sum("amount"), "order_count": measure.count("order_id")},
)
```

Callers then ask for measures by name:

```python
from hypequery.datasets import tenant

result = analytics.for_tenant(tenant("org_123")).execute(
    "orders", {"dimensions": ["country"], "measures": ["revenue"]}
)
```

hypequery plans the SQL, rejects fields the dataset doesn't declare, and adds the tenant filter. A query without a tenant fails instead of reading every customer. The same dataset can be served from FastAPI, consumed by generated React hooks, and exposed to AI agents through the MCP bridge.

## Where each one fits

Use **clickhouse-connect directly** for:

- inserts and ingestion
- schema changes and admin scripts
- one-off analysis where `query_df` on arbitrary SQL is exactly what you want

Use **hypequery** when:

- the same measure is queried from several places: an API, a job, a notebook, a dashboard
- customers see the results, so tenant isolation can't depend on each query remembering a filter
- you want HTTP endpoints, typed frontend hooks, or agent access without writing them by hand

## Trade-offs to know

hypequery returns rows as dictionaries, with decimals, dates, and timestamps as strings so nothing loses precision. That's the right default for APIs. For a notebook, `result.to_pandas()`, `to_polars()` and `to_arrow()` convert a dataset result with column types taken from the dataset definition. For arbitrary SQL that isn't a dataset, `query_df` on the driver is still the direct route.

hypequery is read-only. Inserts stay with the driver.

## Using both

They can share one client. `ClickHouseExecutor` accepts an existing clickhouse-connect client:

```python
import clickhouse_connect
from hypequery.datasets import create_dataset_client
from hypequery.execution import ClickHouseExecutor

from analytics.datasets import registry

client = clickhouse_connect.get_client(host="localhost", username="default", password="")
analytics = create_dataset_client(executor=ClickHouseExecutor(client), registry=registry)
```

Most teams end up with both: the driver for writing and exploring, hypequery for the numbers they share.

posts.title: Tinybird vs ClickHouse Cloud: Is Tinybird More Expensive?
posts.description: Not at the entry level: Tinybird starts at $25/month, while the smallest ClickHouse Cloud service costs about $160/month in compute running around the clock. The pricing side by side, how each one bills, and where each one wins.
posts.body:
Not at the entry level. Tinybird's Developer plan starts at $25/month, and its 0.5 vCPU size costs $49/month with 25 GB of storage and hosted API endpoints included. The smallest ClickHouse Cloud service (Basic, 8 GiB of RAM and 2 vCPUs) costs about $160/month in compute if it runs around the clock, before storage. ClickHouse's own example that keeps it awake 6 hours a day comes to $66.52/month in total. For that money ClickHouse Cloud gives you four times the vCPUs of Tinybird's $49 size, and Tinybird's larger SaaS and Enterprise plans are custom-priced on 12-month credits, so beyond the smallest workloads the cheaper option depends on your hours, data and query rate.

| | Tinybird | ClickHouse Cloud |
|---|---|---|
| Free option | Free plan with no time limit: 0.25 vCPU, 1,000 requests a day, 10 GB of storage | $300 of credits for 30 days |
| Entry paid price | Developer from $25/month; the 0.5 vCPU size is $49/month with 25 GB of storage | Basic, 1 replica of 8 GiB and 2 vCPUs: $159.66/month of compute running 24/7 on AWS us-east-1, plus storage |
| How compute is billed | A plan sized in vCPUs; use above the plan is $0.0002 per vCPU-second | Per minute of active compute: $0.2181 (Basic), $0.2985 (Scale) or $0.3903 (Enterprise) per compute-unit-hour on AWS us-east-1; idle services scale to zero |
| Storage | 25 GB included on Developer, then $0.058/GB | $25.30 per TB-month of compressed data; backups at the same rate |
| Egress | $0.01/GB within a cloud, $0.10/GB between clouds | Public internet from $0.1152/GB, inter-region from $0.0312/GB |
| API hosting | Included: endpoints are the product | Query API endpoints for saved queries, or your own API service, paid separately |
| Larger plans | SaaS and Enterprise, custom-priced on credits with a 12-month commitment | Scale and Enterprise tiers, pay-as-you-go or committed spend |

Prices come from [Tinybird's pricing page](https://www.tinybird.co/pricing), the [ClickHouse Cloud pricing page](https://clickhouse.com/pricing) and the worked examples in [ClickHouse's billing docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/cloud/manage/billing/overview), checked on 9 November 2026. Rates vary by cloud and region.

ClickHouse Cloud is the managed ClickHouse database run by ClickHouse, Inc.: a service with full SQL access over HTTPS, the native protocol and the MySQL wire protocol. Tinybird is a data platform from a separate company that runs ClickHouse underneath and adds ingestion connectors, SQL-to-REST API endpoints, access tokens and a branch-based development workflow. Pick Tinybird when what you want is hosted analytics APIs with as little backend work as possible; pick ClickHouse Cloud when your own services, jobs and BI tools need to read and write a ClickHouse database directly.

## How is Tinybird different from ClickHouse Cloud?

ClickHouse Cloud sells the database as a service, and Tinybird sells a platform built on that database. In ClickHouse Cloud you create tables, run any SQL and connect with any ClickHouse client. In Tinybird you define data sources, pipes and API endpoints as project files or with its [TypeScript SDK](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/quickstarts/typescript-sdk), deploy them to a Workspace, and your application calls the hosted endpoints. Tinybird's [managed ClickHouse page](https://www.tinybird.co/product/managed-clickhouse) says it "runs native ClickHouse under the hood", and it also exposes a ClickHouse HTTP interface, which its [docs](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/query-data/clickhouse-interface) describe as read-only.

| | ClickHouse Cloud | Tinybird |
|---|---|---|
| Run by | ClickHouse, Inc. | Tinybird, which states it is not affiliated with ClickHouse, Inc. |
| What you get | A managed ClickHouse service | Managed ClickHouse plus ingestion, API endpoints, tokens, Cloud Branches and Tinybird Local |
| SQL access | Read and write over HTTPS, native protocol and MySQL wire protocol ([compatibility guide](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/guides/cloud-compatibility)) | API Endpoints and the Query API; the ClickHouse HTTP interface is read-only |
| Ingestion | ClickPipes (billed separately) or any ClickHouse insert path | Events API plus Kafka, S3, GCS and DynamoDB connectors |
| HTTP API from SQL | [Query API endpoints](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/features/sql-console-features/query-endpoints) built from saved queries in the console | API Endpoints are the core of the product |
| Clouds and regions | AWS, Google Cloud and Azure; 38 region codes listed, 21 of them public ([regions](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/reference/supported-regions)) | Regions on AWS and Google Cloud in its docs |
| In your own cloud account | [BYOC](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/guides/infrastructure/deployment-options/byoc/overview), generally available on AWS, GCP and Azure, with a committed contract | [Self-managed regions](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/core-concepts/self-managed), in beta and for development only |
| Free option | $300 of credits for 30 days | Free plan with no time limit |
| Billing unit | Compute-unit-hours plus TB-months of storage | Plan size in vCPUs plus overages; credits on committed plans |

## Is Tinybird more expensive than ClickHouse Cloud?

At the entry level Tinybird costs less in dollars, as the table above shows. Past that it depends on your workload, because the two bill on different units and neither publishes a like-for-like price. ClickHouse Cloud charges for compute time and stored data, so cost follows how many hours your service is awake and how much data you keep. Tinybird charges a plan fee sized in vCPUs and then overages, so cost follows the plan you need to stay inside its limits.

### How ClickHouse Cloud bills

From the [ClickHouse Cloud pricing page](https://clickhouse.com/pricing):

- Compute is metered per minute and billed per compute-unit-hour. One compute unit is 8 GiB of RAM and 2 vCPUs.
- On AWS us-east-1 the listed compute rates are $0.2181 (Basic), $0.2985 (Scale) and $0.3903 (Enterprise) per unit-hour. Rates change with cloud provider and region.
- Storage is $25.30 per TB per month in that region, metered on the compressed size of your data. Backups are billed at the same per-TB rate.
- ClickPipes ingestion and egress are extra: public internet egress starts at $0.1152/GB and inter-region egress at $0.0312/GB. Ingress is free.
- Compute scales to zero when a service is idle, so an intermittent workload stops paying for compute between queries. The cost of that is latency: a paused service has to wake before it answers, and ClickHouse's [idling docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/products/cloud/features/autoscaling/idling) don't recommend it for frequently used customer-facing features.
- New organizations get $300 in credits for 30 days, then move to pay-as-you-go. The pricing page lists no permanent free tier.

### How Tinybird bills

From Tinybird's [pricing page](https://www.tinybird.co/pricing) and [plan docs](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/pricing):

- The Free plan gives 0.25 vCPU, 1,000 requests per day, 10 GB of storage and one query thread, with no time limit. Requests over the burst limit get HTTP 429.
- Developer plans are a fixed monthly fee by size. The pricing page says they start at $25/month and lists the 0.5 vCPU size at $49/month; the plan docs name sizes from S-1/4 (a quarter vCPU) upward. Every size includes 25 GB of storage. Extra storage is $0.058/GB and vCPU use above the plan is $0.0002 per second. Self-service sizes go up to 8 vCPUs.
- SaaS plans run on shared infrastructure from 4 vCPUs, use credits with a 12-month minimum commitment, and bill active minutes, queries per second and storage overages.
- Enterprise plans give you a dedicated ClickHouse cluster with at least 1 TB of storage, also on credits with a 12-month commitment.
- Every plan includes unlimited tables, pipes and endpoints, so hosting the API is part of the fee.

### What decides which one costs less

Tinybird's own FAQ answers the question directly: "For production workloads, it's usually cheaper", on the grounds that it replaces separate ingestion, API and operations work. That is the vendor's claim, so test it against your numbers. The factors that move the result:

- An always-on workload pays ClickHouse Cloud for every hour of compute; an intermittent one benefits from idling. Tinybird's Developer fee is the same either way.
- With ClickHouse Cloud you also pay for wherever your API runs, unless Query API endpoints are enough. Tinybird's fee already covers endpoint hosting.
- For a side project, Tinybird's Free plan costs nothing for as long as you stay inside its limits, while ClickHouse Cloud's trial ends after 30 days or $300, whichever comes first.

Both vendors have estimators: the calculator on the [ClickHouse Cloud pricing page](https://clickhouse.com/pricing) and "Estimate your price" on [Tinybird's pricing page](https://www.tinybird.co/pricing). Put the same data volume and query rate into both before deciding on price.

## Is Tinybird better than ClickHouse?

Tinybird runs ClickHouse, so the useful question is whether its platform layer is better for you than talking to ClickHouse directly. Tinybird is the better choice when hosted endpoints and managed ingestion are most of the work, and ClickHouse Cloud is better when you need the database itself.

Where Tinybird wins:

- A SQL pipe becomes a hosted API endpoint with scoped tokens, without an application server in between.
- Ingestion is built in: the Events API and connectors for Kafka, S3, GCS and DynamoDB.
- The development loop is complete: [Tinybird Local](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/core-concepts/tinybird-local) runs the platform in a container for development, testing and CI, Cloud Branches give shared environments, and the TypeScript and Python SDKs define data sources and endpoints in code.
- The Free plan has no time limit, which suits prototypes and low-traffic features.

Where ClickHouse Cloud wins:

- Any ClickHouse client, BI tool or job can read and write with full SQL. Tinybird's ClickHouse interface is read-only, so writes go through its ingestion paths.
- It covers more ground: AWS, Google Cloud and Azure, with BYOC generally available on all three. Tinybird's self-managed regions are in beta, and its docs say to avoid production workloads on them.
- Idle services stop paying for compute.
- Your DDL uses standard MergeTree engines (Cloud substitutes its SharedMergeTree engine behind the scenes), so the same schema runs on open-source ClickHouse or another host if you move.

## Tinybird vs ClickHouse Cloud: which one should I pick?

Pick Tinybird if:

- The deliverable is analytics APIs, and nobody on the team wants to build and run the serving layer.
- Data arrives from Kafka, S3, GCS, DynamoDB or HTTP events and you want the platform to handle ingestion.
- SQL-focused developers own the analytics, and branches plus a local container fit how they work.
- Consumers only need to read through endpoints or the read-only ClickHouse interface.

Pick ClickHouse Cloud if:

- Services, notebooks, jobs and BI tools all need direct read and write access to ClickHouse.
- Analytics logic should live in your application code and deploy with it, behind your existing auth.
- You need Azure, a specific region, or BYOC for data residency.
- The workload is intermittent enough that scale-to-zero matters, or large enough that you want to tune compute directly.

## Should we use Tinybird in production?

Yes, if your workload fits the plan limits: Tinybird sells its paid plans for production, and its plan docs list SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliance on all plans. The limits worth checking before you commit, all from the [plan docs](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/pricing):

- The Free plan's vCPU limit is hard, and requests over the burst capacity return HTTP 429.
- Developer plans can burst above their vCPU size (3x on the smallest sizes, 2x from S-4 up), and requests beyond the burst also return HTTP 429.
- Each organization is tied to one region; workspaces in another region need a separate organization and plan.
- Self-managed regions are beta and meant for development environments only.

## What are the alternatives to Tinybird, including open source?

The closest alternative is a managed ClickHouse service with your own API layer on top: ClickHouse Cloud, or one of the other hosts in our [comparison of managed ClickHouse services](/blog/managed-clickhouse-services-compared). If you want open source, ClickHouse itself is Apache-2.0 and you can self-host it. Tinybird Local is a development and CI container whose prerequisites include a Tinybird account, so it can't stand in for a self-hosted deployment. If what you liked about Tinybird is turning SQL into HTTP endpoints, ClickHouse Cloud's Query API endpoints do that for saved queries in the console. If you want typed analytics endpoints defined in your own code and served from your own backend, [hypequery](/tinybird-alternative) is an open-source (Apache 2.0) TypeScript and Python layer that runs against any ClickHouse, including ClickHouse Cloud; the [hypequery vs Tinybird comparison](/compare/hypequery-vs-tinybird) covers the trade-offs. It is our product, and it does not ingest data or host anything for you, which Tinybird does.

## TypeScript client for ClickHouse Cloud

The official TypeScript client for ClickHouse Cloud is [`@clickhouse/client`](https://clickhouse.com/docs/integrations/language-clients/js/index) for Node.js, with `@clickhouse/client-web` for browsers and Cloudflare Workers. It talks to ClickHouse over HTTPS (port 8443 on Cloud), using the URL, username and password from the **Connect** dialog in the Cloud console.

```typescript
import { createClient } from '@clickhouse/client';

const client = createClient({
  url: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_URL!, // https://<service>.<region>.<provider>.clickhouse.cloud:8443
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

const result = await client.query({
  query: `
    SELECT event_name, count() AS events
    FROM events
    WHERE tenant_id = {tenant:String} AND occurred_at >= {from:DateTime}
    GROUP BY event_name
    ORDER BY events DESC
  `,
  query_params: { tenant: 'acme', from: '2026-11-01 00:00:00' },
  format: 'JSONEachRow',
  clickhouse_settings: { output_format_json_quote_64bit_integers: 1 },
});

const rows = await result.json<{ event_name: string; events: string }>();
```

`count()` returns a UInt64, which can exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, so the example asks ClickHouse to send 64-bit integers as strings. Set it explicitly: on ClickHouse 26.6 the default is unquoted. With the setting on, the query above returns rows like this (checked on ClickHouse 26.6 with four sample events):

```text
{"event_name":"signup","events":"2"}
{"event_name":"login","events":"1"}
```

The client gives you transport, but you write the row types by hand. [hypequery](/clickhouse-typescript) adds a typed query builder on top: in Node.js it uses `@clickhouse/client` under the hood, generates TypeScript types from your live ClickHouse Cloud schema, and checks table names, columns, filters and result shapes at compile time.

```bash
npm install @hypequery/clickhouse
npm install -D @hypequery/cli
npx hypequery generate   # reads CLICKHOUSE_URL, CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME, CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD, CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE
```

```typescript
import { createQueryBuilder } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './analytics/schema.js';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  url: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_URL!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD!,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});

const rows = await db
  .table('events')
  .select(['event_name'])
  .count('event_id', 'events')
  .where('tenant_id', 'eq', 'acme')
  .where('occurred_at', 'gte', '2026-11-01 00:00:00')
  .groupBy(['event_name'])
  .orderBy('events', 'DESC')
  .execute();
// rows: { event_name: string; events: string }[]
```

hypequery quotes 64-bit integers by default, so `events` is typed and delivered as a string. When a query needs to be an HTTP endpoint, `@hypequery/serve` exposes it with input validation, docs and OpenAPI; the [quick start](/docs/quick-start) covers both steps. That gives you the Tinybird-style "query as an endpoint" result while the endpoint runs in your own application.

If you are on Tinybird, Tinybird documents [connecting `@clickhouse/client`](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/guides/connect-clickhouse-js) to its ClickHouse interface with a workspace token, so the official client also works for reads there.

## Related

- [Managed ClickHouse services compared](/blog/managed-clickhouse-services-compared)
- [ClickHouse with TypeScript](/clickhouse-typescript)
- [hypequery quick start](/docs/quick-start)
- [Building an API on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-api)
- [Real-time analytics on ClickHouse](/clickhouse-real-time-analytics)
- [ClickHouse Cloud pricing](https://clickhouse.com/pricing) and [Tinybird pricing](https://www.tinybird.co/pricing)
- [ClickHouse JavaScript client docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/integrations/language-clients/js/index)
- [Tinybird ClickHouse interface](https://www.tinybird.co/docs/forward/query-data/clickhouse-interface)

posts.title: Migrating from Kysely to hypequery for ClickHouse
posts.description: A practical migration guide for moving ClickHouse queries from Kysely to hypequery: idiom-by-idiom mapping, generated schema types, what you gain, and what you honestly give up.
posts.body:
**Short answer:** migrating Kysely queries to hypequery is mostly mechanical. `db.selectFrom('t')` becomes `db.table('t')`, `.selectAll()` becomes `.select('*')`, SQL operators like `'='` become named operators like `'eq'`, and `.executeTakeFirst()` becomes `.limit(1)` plus destructuring. The one structural change is that you delete your hand-written table interfaces and replace them with a schema generated from your live ClickHouse instance.

This post assumes you've already decided to switch. If you're still evaluating whether hypequery is the right move for your ClickHouse workload, the [hypequery vs Kysely comparison](/compare/hypequery-vs-kysely) covers that decision — this page is the how, not the why.

The migration takes roughly this shape: install and generate types, swap the client, port queries file by file using the mapping table below, then delete the interfaces you used to maintain by hand. The two clients can coexist during the transition, so nothing forces a big-bang rewrite. If you want to see the generated types before committing to porting anything, the [quick start](/docs/quick-start) gets you from install to a typed query in a few minutes.

## Step 1: generate your schema

The biggest day-to-day difference isn't query syntax — it's where your types come from. Running Kysely against ClickHouse (via a community dialect or the MySQL wire protocol) means writing the `Database` interface yourself:

```ts
// Kysely on ClickHouse: hand-maintained, hand-guessed
interface OrdersTable {
  id: string;
  tenant_id: number;
  region: string;
  status: string;
  total: number;      // is this what ClickHouse actually returns? (often no)
  created_at: Date;   // ClickHouse returns a string over HTTP
}

interface Database {
  orders: OrdersTable;
}
```

These interfaces drift from the real schema, and worse, they encode what you *assume* ClickHouse returns rather than what it actually returns. hypequery replaces them with introspection:

```bash
npx hypequery generate
# connects to ClickHouse, introspects your tables, writes generated/schema.ts
```

Re-run `npx hypequery generate` whenever the schema changes. The generated types encode ClickHouse's runtime behavior over HTTP: `UInt64` comes back as a **string** in JavaScript (it can exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`), `DateTime` comes back as a formatted string, and `Nullable(T)` becomes `T | null`. If your Kysely interfaces typed a `UInt64` column as `number`, you had a latent precision bug — the generated schema makes that class of mistake unrepresentable. The [ClickHouse TypeScript guide](/clickhouse-typescript) goes deeper on these mappings.

## Step 2: swap the client

```ts
import { createQueryBuilder } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';
import type { IntrospectedSchema } from './generated/schema.js';

const db = createQueryBuilder<IntrospectedSchema>({
  url: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_URL!,
  username: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_USERNAME!,
  password: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_PASSWORD,
  database: process.env.CLICKHOUSE_DATABASE!,
});
```

This talks to ClickHouse over its native HTTP interface via `@clickhouse/client` — no dialect adapter, no MySQL-compat port.

## The idiom mapping table

| Kysely | hypequery |
|---|---|
| `db.selectFrom('orders')` | `db.table('orders')` |
| `.selectAll()` | `.select('*')` |
| `.select(['region', 'status'])` | `.select(['region', 'status'])` |
| `.where('status', '=', 'completed')` | `.where('status', 'eq', 'completed')` |
| `.where('total', '>=', 100)` | `.where('total', 'gte', 100)` |
| `.where('region', 'in', regions)` | `.where('region', 'in', regions)` |
| `fn.sum('total').as('revenue')` | `.sum('total', 'revenue')` |
| `.innerJoin('users', 'users.id', 'orders.user_id')` | `.innerJoin('users', 'user_id', 'users.id')` |
| `.orderBy('created_at', 'desc')` | `.orderBy('created_at', 'DESC')` |
| `.executeTakeFirst()` | `.limit(1)` + `.execute()`, then destructure |
| `` sql`...` `` template tag | `selectExpr()`, `rawAs()`, `raw()` helpers |
| Hand-written `Database` interface | Generated `IntrospectedSchema` |

The operator strings are the change your fingers will notice most. hypequery uses named operators — `eq`, `neq`, `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte`, `in`, `notIn`, `like`, `between` — instead of SQL symbols. They autocomplete, and the value side is type-checked against the column, so `where('total', 'between', ...)` demands a two-element tuple. The full list is in the [filter operators guide](/blog/clickhouse-filter-operators-typescript).

## Porting a typical query

A representative Kysely aggregation:

```ts
// Kysely
const revenue = await db
  .selectFrom('orders')
  .select(({ fn }) => [
    'region',
    fn.sum('total').as('revenue'),
    fn.count('id').as('order_count'),
  ])
  .where('status', '=', 'completed')
  .where('created_at', '>=', startDate)
  .groupBy('region')
  .orderBy('revenue', 'desc')
  .execute();
```

The hypequery equivalent:

```ts
// hypequery
const revenue = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select(['region'])
  .sum('total', 'revenue')
  .count('id', 'order_count')
  .where('status', 'eq', 'completed')
  .where('created_at', 'gte', startDate)
  .groupBy('region')
  .orderBy('revenue', 'DESC')
  .execute();
```

Aggregations move from Kysely's expression-builder callback to first-class chained methods that take `(column, alias)`. Beyond `sum`/`count`, the builder ships `avg`, `min`, `max`, `countDistinct`, `quantile`, `stddev`, `variance`, and ClickHouse's `argMax`/`argMin` — that last pair has no Kysely equivalent short of raw SQL.

## The executeTakeFirst() habit

The method Kysely users reach for reflexively doesn't exist in hypequery. The replacement is one extra line:

```ts
// Kysely
const order = await db
  .selectFrom('orders')
  .selectAll()
  .where('id', '=', orderId)
  .executeTakeFirst();

// hypequery
const [order] = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select('*')
  .where('id', 'eq', orderId)
  .limit(1)
  .execute();
// order: OrderRow | undefined — same contract as executeTakeFirst()
```

The `.limit(1)` matters: without it, ClickHouse scans and returns every matching row and you throw away all but the first in application code. Array destructuring gives you the same `T | undefined` shape `executeTakeFirst()` returned, so downstream null-checks port unchanged. There's a dedicated post on this pattern, including the `executeTakeFirstOrThrow` equivalent, at [executeTakeFirst() in hypequery](/blog/clickhouse-executetakefirst-hypequery).

## Raw SQL escape hatches

Where you used Kysely's `sql` template tag inside a select, hypequery's standalone helpers do the same job:

```ts
import { selectExpr } from '@hypequery/clickhouse';

const ranked = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select([
    'region',
    selectExpr('ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY total DESC)', 'rank'),
  ])
  .execute();
```

`selectExpr(sql, alias)` covers aliased expressions, `rawAs` and `raw` cover the rest. One honest note: window functions are not first-class builder methods in hypequery — `selectExpr` with an `OVER (...)` clause is the supported path, same as it was with Kysely's template tag.

## What you gain

**ClickHouse clauses Kysely never modeled.** These are native builder methods, not string escapes:

```ts
// Top 3 orders per region — ClickHouse LIMIT BY, no window function needed
const top3 = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select(['region', 'id', 'total'])
  .orderBy('total', 'DESC')
  .limitBy(3, 'region')
  .execute();

// Deduplicated reads from a ReplacingMergeTree
const current = await db
  .table('orders')
  .select('*')
  .final()
  .where('tenant_id', 'eq', tenantId)
  .execute();

// PREWHERE: filter cheap columns before reading wide ones
const events = await db
  .table('events')
  .select(['event_type', 'properties'])
  .prewhere('tenant_id', 'eq', tenantId)
  .where('event_type', 'eq', 'page_view')
  .execute();
```

Add `.groupByTimeInterval('created_at', '1 day')` for time-series bucketing, `.withTotals()`, `.settings()`, and `.withCTE()` for typed CTEs. With Kysely, each of these was a raw-SQL fragment or simply unavailable.

**Layers above the builder.** Kysely stops at the query. hypequery's optional packages continue upward: `@hypequery/serve` turns queries into validated HTTP routes with zod input schemas and OpenAPI docs, and `@hypequery/react` provides TanStack Query hooks against those routes. If your Kysely queries currently feed hand-rolled Express endpoints and hand-typed fetch calls, this is where the migration pays for itself twice.

**Types that match the wire.** Covered above, but it's the compounding win: every ported query gets result types that reflect what ClickHouse actually sends, not what an interface author hoped.

## What you lose — honestly

**Multi-dialect portability.** Kysely speaks Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, and MSSQL from one API. hypequery is ClickHouse-only, by design. If one Kysely codebase was serving both your OLTP database and ClickHouse, you'll now run two libraries — which is the standard pattern anyway (Kysely or Prisma for OLTP, a ClickHouse-native layer for analytics), but it is one more dependency.

**Transactions.** Kysely's `db.transaction().execute(...)` has no hypequery equivalent. ClickHouse itself doesn't offer meaningful multi-statement transactions, so you weren't getting real transactional semantics through Kysely on ClickHouse either — but if any of your Kysely code relied on transactions, that code belongs on your OLTP database, not in this migration.

**The plugin ecosystem.** Kysely's plugin system (camelCase conversion, community plugins), its migration tooling, and its breadth of community dialects have no counterpart here. hypequery's surface is narrower and ClickHouse-shaped. If your workflow leaned on Kysely plugins for cross-cutting query transforms, budget time to replace those behaviors explicitly.

If any of these are dealbreakers, that's a signal to revisit the [comparison page](/compare/hypequery-vs-kysely) rather than push through the migration.

## A migration checklist

1. `npx hypequery generate` — introspect the schema, inspect it, compare against your hand-written interfaces (expect to find drift).
2. Create the hypequery client alongside your Kysely instance. Both can run in the same process.
3. Port one query module at a time using the mapping table. The compiler flags every column typo and operator mismatch as you go.
4. Grep for `executeTakeFirst` and convert each site to `.limit(1)` + destructure.
5. Grep for `` sql` `` usages and convert to `selectExpr`/`rawAs`/`raw` — then check whether `limitBy`, `final`, `prewhere`, or `groupByTimeInterval` eliminates the raw SQL entirely.
6. Delete the hand-written `Database` interface. Wire `npx hypequery generate` into CI so schema drift fails the build instead of surfacing in production.

## Where to go from here

- [Quick start](/docs/quick-start) — install, introspect, first typed query.
- [ClickHouse query builder guide](/clickhouse-query-builder) — the full builder surface beyond what this migration touched.
- [ClickHouse + React](/clickhouse-react) — the hooks layer, if you're replacing hand-typed fetch calls next.
- [Building a ClickHouse API](/clickhouse-api) — turning ported queries into governed HTTP routes with @hypequery/serve.
